speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
A number of petitions have been received, covering a period of some months past, from the lighthouse keepers in different parts of the country asking for an increase in their salaries. At the present time lighthouse keepers are divided into different classes, with fixed salaries for each class, starting at the minimum, and advancing by certain gradations up to the

maximum. The request from these different classes is that the minimum be increased. The petitions have received consideration, but I cannot at the. present time give any assurance to my hon. friend such as he asks for.

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
In the early part of the debate, there was a discussion as to the number of officers who had been engaged in recruiting in Quebec. I did not at that time delay the House with the names of those officers; in fact I did not know the names of all the gentlemen whom we had engaged in. recruiting in that province; but I have here a list-it is not a complete list-of a number of very excellent officers who were in service at that time and who did yeoman work so far as they could.
In British Columbia we had as District Officer Commanding, Col. Roy, a French-Canadian who was in command in the English-speaking district. This officer found favour on every hand, no one finding fault with him. In Toronto we had General Les-sard. There was another Roy, an officer of the Engineers, who did recruiting work in the early part of the war, and who went over with the 22nd Battalion, and who, as was mentioned here by the Prime Minister, gave up his life in trying to save some of his comrades from a bomb explosion in one of the trenches. There are two Col. Fages, both very excellent officers, each of whom has done his best in recruiting work. Then there is Col. Louis LeDuc, who is well known to us and who has become a Brigadier in the service. Col. Gaudette, who was in charge of the Dominion Arsenal for many years and who retired, again came to the front and did excellent recruiting work. He went over with the 22nd Battalion, but his health failed him. He now occupies a very high position in munitions work in England. Col. Papineau is a young lad who went over as a lieutenant in the Princess Patricia's and who was promoted to a colonelcy in the service. He is one of the finest officers to be found in the force. There is also a Captain Papineau who has done splendid work in recruiting and who has also served in the war. Col. Paquette of Quebec gave his time recruiting throughout the Quebec district. There are two or three Panets, only one of whom is in Quebec. Col. Labelle has done what he can. Col. Landry has done good work both in Quebec and at the front. Col. Ostel, of the 65th Battalion was unable, on account of his state of health, to go to the front, but he has been one of the best recruiting officers. He has enlisted many boys, all of whom have done very well. Col. Chauveau, of Quebec, and Col. Puize of Rimouski together raised one of the finest battalions that have gone to the

front. They have done fine service in the way of recruiting for that battalion. Col. Puize is regarded as a very fine officer. Col. Dansereau, a Royal Military College graduate, did splendid service under Col. Currie at the battle of St. Julien. He was an old Montreal boy. Col. Gingras has been at the front and has done splendid work. He has been back to Canada for recruiting work and is recruiting in the United States at the present time. Col. Barre all know as one of the most fearless and successful officers at the front. Major Asselin, who declined to take command of a battalion on account of his not having previous military experience, is a most experienced recruiting officer. Col. Lepro-hon, who went over with the First Contingent, was wounded and came back. He went to the Northwest and raised another battalion, not quite to full strength, and it has gone overseas. Then there is a Col. De Salaberry, who, I understand, is a descendant of the famous De Salaberry who went over with the Princess Patricia's and returned to take the command of a battalion. He has gone back with his battalion. Col. Hector Verret has done yeoman service at the front and now commands a battalion there. Col. Readman, who was given an opportunity of raising a battalion, did his level best and succeeded in raising a certain number of men. Col. Blois, a man po-ssibly a little over age, but a most enthusiastic gentleman, also went to the front and did his work to the satisfaction, at all events, of many of his officers over there. He has come back from the front and has done his best in recruiting. Col. Grothe has also done good work. Col. Tremblay, commander of the 22nd, is a most excellent officer and a splendid soldier. Col. Plante has also done good work. There are two Col. Scotts, who have been over and have come back again, who are engaged in recruiting work at the present time. Then there is Major Dubuc, and then last, but by no means least, the Laviolettes. I am speaking from recollection. I think there are two or three Lavio-lette boys, one of whom was severely wounded and is now, I am sorry to say, dying at Montreal, another who was wounded at the front, and a third boy who has done yeoman work. These soldiers have all done splendid work in the way of recruiting.

speechtext: I do not want to go into details or to criticise any particular plan of recruiting, but I am bound to say that those of us connected with the militia can feel on looking back that we are entitled to pat ourselves on the back, because our system was the best of all. I did not find platform recruiting very effective. Our officers with their recruiting committee reached eviery part of the Dominion, and had they been consulted they would have produced as fine a list-a voter's list, you may call it if you like-of eligible young men from the Atlantic to the Pacific as it was possible to compile. They had lists of the eligible young men in every district of the country, and there were very few of military age in Canada who did not have the opportunity of putting on the uniform if they chose to do so.

I also know Colonel Paquet, who is a son of the ex-postmaster of Quebec city, who was one of rhy officials when I was Postmaster General. He is a charming young fellow, very active, and very able, and he was most anxious to have his regiment go to the front. He raised two regiments, and what happened? I might inform the
committee that the Asselin regiment was raised in less than two months. We received all the necessary aid and backing from the department, and if the same aid and backing had been given in connection with recruiting in other parts of the province of Quebec many an Asselin regiment would have been raised. Major Asselin, it is only just to say, is an exceedingly brilliant French Canadian, pne of the most popular men in the province of Quebec, and it is not surprising that he succeeded in surrounding himself with young officers of ability, some of whom had been recalled from the front to help in the formation of that regiment.

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The hon. member must bear in mind that in every battalion area in the province of Quebec we did not have an Asselin or a Lemieux. I took the liberty the other day of suggesting that members wishing to make suggestions on the Bill should put them in concise form, and I should now like to present to the committee a few notes I have made.

On section 4-calling out by classes:
4. (1) The Governor In Council may from time to time by proqlamation call out on active service as aforesaid for the defence of Canada, either in Canada or beyond Canada, any class or subclass of men described in section three and all men within the class or subclass so called out shall, from the date of such proclamation, be deemed to be soldiers enlisted in the Military Forces of Canada and subject to military law for the duration of the present war, and of demobilization thereafter, save as hereinafter provided.
(2)	Men so called out shall report and shall be placed on active service in the Canadian Expeditionary Force as may be set out in such proclamation or in regulations, but until so placed on active service, shall be deemed to be on leave of absence without pay.
(3)	Any man by or in respect of whom an application for exemption is made as hereinafter provided, shall, so long as such application or any appeal in connection therewith is pending and during the currency of any exemption granted him, be deemed to be on leave of absence without pay.
(4)	Any man who is called out and who, without reasonable excuse, fails to report as aforesaid or to remain on active service where placed shall be guilty, according to the circumstances, of desertion, or of absenting himself without leave and shall be liable
(a)	to be tried by court-martial and convicted and punished by imprisonment, for a term not exceeding three years, or
(b)	on summary conviction to imprisonment for any term not exceeding three years.
I prefer the Militia Act as better, more elastic, more workable, less inclined to cause friction, and more inclined to produce good results, but the Government does not so consider it.
I,	therefore, will not take one minute in discussing that aspect of the question, merely placing myself on record. I shall loyally support any and every proposition enacted in the Bill when finally completed; and shall, with the least delay, freely give my suggestions.
My preferences are more or less well known.-
1.	The tribunals are non-military, and are under the administration of the Justice Department. My suggestion would be to place them under military control, but let their composition be non-military.
2.	A mere suggestion is, the area unit, instead of being provincial, should be military district.
3.	There should be no special exemptions for "financiers" more than for farmers.
4.	It would have been advisable to have had registration.
5.	Clergy should not be exempt.
6.	Section 11, subsection (e) is the only one to my mind that should be retained. Is there a man in Canada who may not

be exempted under section 11 as it now stands?
7.	Desertions. It might be well to' provide for punishment under this, and other sections of the Bill, at the front.
8.	But, believing the intention of the Government is to help enlistment, and feeling that it is not meant merely to inflame one section against another, I will give every support, consideration and assistance to the passage, and to the carrying out of the principles of the Bill. It should be law within a week. My one aim is to help, uphold, and upbuild the gallant fellows who are enduring so patiently and performing so nobly at the front.
I regret taking up the time of the House with another matter, important not in itself but in its bearing on the whole public situation, that is, the falling off in recruiting, the causes thereof, and the denials of certain statements made.
The situation from February, 1916, to the autumn of tftat year was unique. Men were enlisting up till February and March as they never did before in any land. The home locality plan worked well.
Then the Prime Minister, as well as the Minister of Militia, was daily, sometimes hourly, worried by a fictitious agitation-I use the term "fictitious;" it was a very nasty agitation. Suggestions, complaints, advice, appeals, demands, re recruiting were made.
Possibly more than any other, except the Finance Minister, the influence of Lord Sbaughnessy was potent in this embarrassment. Both Lord Shaughnessy and Sir Thomas White complained of the number of battalions being raised in Montreal and Toronto respectively at the same time. In the Montreal area, with a total population of nearly a million, including the adjoining counties, there were being recruited three battalions. On our basis of 40,000 for a battalion of 1,000 there should have been at least twenty to twenty-one instead of three. In Toronto there were five, or including two formerly authorized but fully completed, only seven were under way, where, as compared with the country districts, there should have been twelve. From one or other of these two gentlemen the fol- ' lowing fallacious arguments were also advanced :
"Industries would be ruined if so many men were enlisted;"
"Farmers could not put in their crops;"
"Munitions could not be made;"
"The war "would be over by July or August, 1916;"

"Transports could not be had;"
"It would take «a long time to get the troops to England, as only a certain number could be taken- monthly."

By whom were those
statements made?

By one or other of
these gentlemen, and 'by others, of course. Every -one had them in his mouth.
1.	From first to last the tendency of the cry was not the upholding and strengthening of the boys at the front so much as the commercial idea at home. The Prime Minister certainly was worried, and be his recollection whatever it may of any particular conference, it is apparent from the results what was running through bis mind. He was interviewed by Mr. Godfrey, of Toronto, w'ho, later, spoke of it to the Chairman of the Toronto Recruiting Association, who, in turn, reported to his Association. The data may have been more or less expanded or contracted, but in general terms it appears that the Prime Minister entertained the idea early in the spring of 1916 of stopping recruiting, and that he felt inclined to stop it but for the fear that it could not be resurrected.
2.	That large numbers were then already enrolled and in training in Canada.
3.	That the demands and needs of labour must be regarded.
4.	That transports were not available t-o carry all the troops, and, at the rate of moving them, there were -men enough enrolled to keep the transports busy for many months.
5.	It was hoped the war would be over by August, 1916.
Such were the impressions given as coming from Mr. Godfrey, through the chairman, to the members of the Toronto Recruiting Association. Whether Mr. Godfrey got them all from the Prime Minister or from some other source is 'not given to the public.
Further, I assert, that influences and statements were utilized to the effect that, as Minister of Militia, I was merely forming battalions and recruiting men who would never he used, and all for my own vainglory. I did not learn until later that jealousy, envy, and overweening ambition were actuating those working against the be-st interests of the great cause.
I leave it to the people of Canada and to the boys at the front to determine who has worked disinterestedly for the soldiers and the cause, and who for vainglory.
On Saturday last, I observe from Hansard, that Sir Thomas White denied he had ever used to me the words " Canada has already done her full duty to England in recruiting in this war." The Finance Minister on two occasions used the expresion to me; on one occasion he put it in the form pf a question, prefacing it with the words " don't you think?" etc. On the second occasion he made the distinct statement. On another occasion, not to me, he went farther, and instead of using the identical words " full duty " the expression was " more than her fuli duty." On the second occasion, I assured him it was not for England but for Canada, for the Empire, and for human liberty that I was in the war. On Saturday last, the Finance Minister quoted a letter to a Toronto gentleman; I do not know whether it was written in 1917 or in 1916-both dates are somewhat mixed up in the report; but np matter when it was written, it hears on its face the imprint that the soldiers in the trenches are secondary to the commercial interests.
I need make no apology here, or elsewhere, regarding my loyalty to the business interests of Canada. When the hon. the Finance Minister had Canada on the verge of financial ruin, at the beginning of the war, my loyalty to their cause was then shown by my actions in establishing industries in Canada which resulted in placing her industries of every class on a sound financial basis; but I have never made any pretence of placing anything on a par with the soldiers in the trenches. They stand first in the heart of every honest Canadian. The Finance Minister's letter in every reference places them secondary.
Considerable interest is evidently manifesting itself on the general aspect of this case. From one of the most distinguished men high in the ranks of the Conservative party in Canada-I may say very high in the ranks of the Conservative party, and one who will be a good deal higher still-one concerning whose loyalty to the party or to the great cause is unquestioned, I have received a report of which the following is an extract:
Let us look back to 1911, when the piteous, agonizing cry for help was heard from what is now historically known as the anxious, financial, and commercial group, who with the erstwhile protector of 'Nabob's vineyard' urged to the front on their behalf-and who with tearful voice apologizing for his desertion from his party-pleaded for the success of his new and untried love, so that the interests of his superiors could be saved and protected; and then we can understand all that has happened since.
Not satisfied with the saving grace that the party at that time so unctuously threw around

them they have ever since been using* their advocate for their own personal gains; and this Government was never satisfactory to them until their interests have been made paramount.
Not even the exigencies of this horrible war were overlooked or unexploited; for, even here, their interests have been served; and some day he who could have been served-and there is none so blind as he who will not see-will see in all its hideousness a wreck which constant and never-ceasing intrigue has made. But he will have for his comfort, if comfort it can be, the sight of others who have been similarly betrayed; for slowly, but surely, Ephraim is returning to his idols and his recantation will soon be due.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me most positively assure this House and the country of the absolute truth of the statements which I have made.
Has the Prime Minister nothing to say in answer to the statement of my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes) ?
I am not making any statement with regard to the Prime Minister at all.	[DOT]
I asked if the Government has anything to say.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The statement
is already made. I have nothing more to add. I am perfectly convinced in my own mind as to what the facts were. I have already stated them to the House, and I repeat them again
On section 4:
Sir \\ ILI RID LAURIER:	We considered the first three paragraphs of this section the other day and, as far as I am concerned, I have nothing further to add; but, the fourth paragraph requires some explanation:
Any man who is called out and who, without reasonable excuse, fails to report as aforesaid or to remain on active service where placed shall be guilty, according to the circumstances, of desertion, or of absenting himself without leave and shall be liable
(a)	to be tried by court martial and convicted and punished by imprisonment, for a term not exceeding three years, or
(b)	on summary conviction to imprisonment for any term not exceeding three years.
By this section concurrent jurisdiction is given to have a court-martial or to take proceedings in an ordinary magistrate's court. Is that correct?
That is correct, but I do not think the word " concurrent " is quite right; it is alternative jurisdiction.

Why should there be two recourses instead of one? It seems to me that trial before a magistrate ought to be quite enough. A man is called and he immediately becomes a soldier. Then, he claims his exemption; it is either admitted or not, and if his claim is rejected and he does not report, he is liable to be taken before the court. Would it not be better to have him taken before a magistrate rather than to have a court-martial?

There are various circumstances and it is thought better to make the jurisdiction alternative for that reason. For example, if a man fails to leave his ordinary avocation and to report for duty, it would appear to me as much more convenient, and indeed more fitting, that his case should be tried before a magistrate. He has never physically come under military jurisdiction. On the other hand, a man might come within the military jurisdiction and fail to accept the assignment to such military duty as he might be allotted to. He has come physically under military jurisdiction and -the more convenient method would be to prosecute him by court-martial. Subsection 4 provides for taking care of both contingencies and consequently alternative jurisdiction is established.

Very well;
that is satisfactory. Who is to prosecute? If he is brought before a magistrate, as under the ordinary law, can anybody become an informer and prosecutor and lay a complaint against him?

If a man is convicted and sentenced to the full term of three years, is it intended that he shall be confined in the county jail of the county in which the action is carried on? If so, it would seem to me to be a very improper Diace to imprison a man for such a long term. Most of the jails are insanitary, there is no way of giving the prisoner exercise, and no opportunity of putting him at work. Rather than put a man in jail for three years without an opportunity of getting fresh air, it would be better to put him against the wall at once and shoot him. There is another question in connection with this that I would like to submit to my hon. friend and that is the question of municipal expense. Will the board of the prisoner become a charge on the county where the trial is held? Under the present system of summary conviction, as you know, the expense falls on the county. It strikes me that there should be some provision by which the expenses would be borne by the Department of Militia and Defence in order that it should not fall on the county in a case where the prisoner is a military prisoner.

In the first place, I
need only call my hon. friend's attention to the law of the land which prevents imprisonment in any county jail for two years or upwards. I. think my hon. friend will recall that two years less one day is the limit of confinement in any other institution than a penitentiary. If the full term, of two years or upwards, were given, the confinement would necessarily not be in the county jail. As to the municipality, the county or other party bearing	the expense, I would like to
hear the reason of my hon friend for feeling that there should be any different law applied here for violations of this Act from what would be applied for violations of any Act. My hon. friend will recall that in almost innumerable statutes, and in a great many Orders in Council passed under the authority of statutes, there appears the very same clause as appears here. Offences are created, offences are punishable on summary conviction and the
penalty is there stated. Under the law of the land the expense falls where it falls.
It would appear to me that there can be no good reason advanced why it should not fall here as in innumerable other cases.
Is there any appeal?

The summary conviction provisions of the Criminal Code would apply where there is an appeal.
Mr. MARCIL.: I am not familiar with the Code. If a man is condemned to three years' imprisonment, is there an appeal to a higher court?

There are the summary trial provisions of the Code, and there are the summary conviction provisions.. My recollection is that there are cases under the summary conviction provisions in which there is an appeal.
There is no appeal except in stated cases.
Whatever it is-I do not pretend to be able to give every portion of it to the House offhand, but I think there are cases in which appeals are allowed. The general law will apply.
This shopld be made very clear now.
It is very clear right now, and it has been long established in the Criminal Code.
I think appeals should be allowed in these cases, because it is a very serious matter to take a man out of his ordinary occupation and put him in jail for three years without the right of appeal.

My hon. friend will remember that under the summary convictions clauses of the Code three years is by no means the maximum penalty that may fall on a man who comes under those provisions. I have known cases under summary conviction of much longer imprisonment than that. So, whatever reasons for appeal there may be here, there would be as strong reasons in other cases. Thus the general law applies. I do not see what more could be asked for.
Does the hon. gentleman mean that in these cases there will be no appeal?
I do not mean that at all.

We ought to know distinctly.

Mr. MARCH,: The people are deeply interested in this clause, and all possible information that could be given should now be forthcoming in order to clear up this misunderstanding. The people are not very familiar with this kind of legislation, and any information that could be given would be of great advantage. We should know whether or not there is any appeal in these cases.
I shall make a statement, later, on the subject of appeals under the summary convictions clauses. I am not clear at the present time.
I think you will find that there is an appeal under the summary convictions clauses of the Code, straight to'the county court judge.
An appeal from a court martial?
No, from summary conviction.
But these men are sent to jail by court martial.
1 do not know what would be done there, but on summary conviction there is an appeal to the county court judge, practically a re-trial.

In case of a court martial, the judgment of the court is always subject to revision by the military authorities, and that is really an appeal; and so, if what my hon. friend (Mr. Car-veil) says is right, there is always a re-trial.

Speaking, not on the details of the vvorking out of the clause but on the clause itself, it strikes me that the punishment is too light. As I read subsection 4, it is dealing with two classes cf cases, one where a man fails to report, aqd the other where he has been on active service and deserts. It seems to me that the punishment of three years in the latter case particularly, is utterly inadequate to the offence of desertion after being on active service. The punishment from all time for desertion has been much more severe, and I do 4 p.m. not know why it should be reduced to three years in a critical time like this. If all is true that has been said about a certain class who have been denominated slackers, to send them to jail for three years would be like sending them to a picnic; they would rather welcome the safe incarceration in either a county jail or a penitentiary if they could be safe from going to war. My idea is to make the 
public understand that this law is a drastic measure, and so I think that this punishment should be ten years instead of three for the man who deserts and probably five for the man who fails to report. I feel that it is the sense of the loyal element pf the country at large that whatever this Bill shall be it shall be drastic and intended to meet the case. Those who are unwilling to do their duty, or who fail to do it after undertaking it, should be met by a Bill that is drastic in every phase. This Bill should be held up to them now as something that will reach them and reach them hard. In that way many of them may come in before the terms of this Bill are passed into law.

I am not as anxious as the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Morphy) to have a drastic measure, but we ought to have a clear measure and to know exactly where we are. This very clause leads us into a good deal of confusion. By the first section of the Act, we have made the Army Act part of this Bill. The Army Act upon this point is far more severe than my hon. friend from Perth has suggested this Bill should be. Here is section 12 of the Army Act:
Every person subject to military law who commits any of the following offences ; that is to say,
(a)	Deserts or attempts to desert His Majesty's Service; or,
(b)	Persuades, endeavours to persuade, procures or attempts to procure any person subject to military law to desert from His Majesty's service, shall, on conviction by court-martial, if he committed such offence when on active service or under orders for active service, be liable to suffer death, or such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned.
If the Army Act is incorporated in this Bill, and it already is incorporated by the first section of this Bill, under the Army Act, a person charged with the offence of desertion is 'liable to suffer death. It must be remembered that under the chapter I have read the punishment of death is applicable when the man is called to active service. In former years the punishment for desertion was death in all cases, in peace time and in war time; but in later years it has been made applicable only during active service. Under the section we are now considering it is provided:
The Governor in Council may from time to time by proclamation call out on active service-
The man who is called out under this Bill, if it becomes law, is held to be on active service, and therefore, if the Army Act is incorporated in this Bill, as it al-

.ready is by the first section, the deserter is liable to the ,punishment of death. It is true that under this section he is liable only to imprisonment fot three years. That is a provision of this Bill. But the Bill has already made the Army Act a part of the law which is to be, and I cannot see how we can escape the conclusion that desertion is punishable by death.

By section 13 it is clearly shown that this Act is by itself, although I believe there is a misprint in the ward " therewith."
The Militia Act, the Army Act, and the King's Regulations and Orders for the Army shall so far as applicable and not inconsistent therewith

	t
I think that is a clerical error and means " not inconsistent herewith."
-apply to and form part of this Act.
That clearly takes the Army Act and the Militia Act and the King's Regulations and Orders out of this Act where they are inconsistent with its terms.

I do not say
to the contrary, but at all events we should know where we >are. Is the Army Act to apply or not to apply?
Sir ROBERT jBORDEN: It seems to me very simple. The Army Act is to apply so far .as applicable and where it is not inconsistent with this Act.

That is so
intended?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In respect to
these particular offences it would be inconsistent, and therefore this Act would prevail.

Would it not be advisable to include as a schedule to the Bill the clauses of the Army Act that do apply, because the people .generally are not like members of this House or of the legal profession or of the military profession; they are not familiar with ail these things.. Would it not be well to add the clauses to the Army Act, so as to know exactly what applies and what does not apply, so that every man to whom this Bill may be sent will know exactly what he was up against?

There is no possibility of doing that. It could be done better by a provision in the clause. There is a certain application of the Army Act, but it must not be applied so as to conflict with this clause. For example, when a man is
tried by court martial, the principles that govern such tribunals apply, and the Army Act applies; but when it comes to the penalty, this Act applies. The tribunal cannot go beyond the limit fixed by this Act.
If one were to extract clauses, he could not extract the clauses that apply to court martial, because that is governed by the provisions of this Bill. On the question of an appeal under summary conviction, I would refer to section 749 and section 146 of the Criminal Code. Those sections are in pretty full terms and set out the provisions for the appeal. Later on, in section 761, are to be found the provisions for stating a case. It will, therefore, appear that such provision for appeal is made here as has been considered in the general run of criminal convictions.

I have read clause 12, which my hon. friend referred to, but it does not give much information. It says that the regulations are to be made by the Governor in Council. That is one thing I do not like. I think the regulations should be set forth in the Act, and made part of , the statute. The advertisement or notice which shall be given of that proclamation depends entirely on the view of the Governor in Council. You are going to punish a man who is called out under subsection 4 of section 4, who without reasonable excuse fails to report. Many people in the country do not read the papers. Nobody reads the Canada Gazette. Members of Parlianjent are the only gentlemen who receive it, and they throw it in the waste-paper basket.
That might be a reasonable excuse.

It might be. That
would depend entirely on the view of the magistrate. All magistrates are very mortal-some more so than others-and I would not like the community at large to be subject to the whim of the magistrate, or to be subject always to the whim of the county judge. Therefore, I think it should be distinctly stated in this Bill what the advertisement for the proclamation should be. All I want to do is to have the Bill in reasonable shape, so that the public will be protected from prosecution. I do not imagine the intention of the Government is to persecute in any way, but still . the tribunals might.

Of course, if regulations were embodied in the Bill, then they would not be regulations. They would be

sections of the Bill. Wherever regulations are referred to in any Act, they are to be afterwards promulgated by the authorities designated by the Act. That is the nature of regulations. As to publication, I may say that we embody as much in the Bill as can reasonably be done, and more than is done in England. In the Bill, we leave less to regulation than is done under the British Act. For example, under the British Act there is no division.
Pardon me, I do not care anything about the British Act. We are dealing with this country.

Perhaps other hon.
gentlemen do.
I am not speaking for other hon. gentlemen.

In the British Act they leave these provisions to be afterwards worked out by regulation. Here we specify the division. As to publication, the reason it is put in the shape it is in Section 12 is that some notices and some regulations, which from time to time may be made necessary, will be of such very minor importance and such purely local consequence that it would be unwise to provide in the Bill that all of them should receive the same publicity, and that we should go to the same expense with regard to all. There may be regulations later on which will provide for the case of a tribunal whose head resides three or four . miles from where hearings are held for the convenience of the public. It would not require the same publicity that other more general regulations would require. Consequently, it has to be left to the discretion of those who are most directly interested in the success of the Bill to see that such publicity is given as will bring the provisions of the Bill, and the provisions of the regulation, home to all to whom they should be brought home.

I suggest to the Solicitor General the desirability of providing a different tribunal for the case of a man who has actually been enrolled and gone into active service and becomes a deserter, from the tribunal which is to try the case of a young man who simply fails to report. That is along the line followed by the hon. gentleman from North Perth (Mr. Morphy), though, of course, he dealt more with the punishment. It seems to me very objectionable that a young man who is simply called out by the proclamation should be liable to be tried by court martial. If he 
is tried by court martial there is no appeal, and the question as to whether he had a reasonable excuse or not would be a question of fact in regard to which a young man should have the opportunity of appealing, if the decision was, in his opinion, contrary to the facts of the case. Therefore, I think that trial by court martial ought to 'be limited to the case of one who deserts after he -has actually become attached to the army and engaged upon active service in Canada, of course, as well as abroad. A proclamation issues, we will say, calling upon young men between the ages of 20 and 23 to come forward and report. A young man may not come within that class. He may be, according to his own belief and the belief of his parents, 24 years of age. He may not be one who is liable to report under the first call. It would be a very great hardship if he should be brought before a court martial, tried .and convicted as a deserter under this Act, when, according to his belief and the belief of his parents, he was not entitled to be called at all.
^ Mr. MEIGHEN: That would come under " reasonable excuse."

But the court martial may decide he was under 24 years of age, and that he had no reasonable excuse for not coming forward. It would be a very great hardship that he should be convicted and sentenced to three years in the penitentiary by court martial, without having any right of appeal. There is no provision whatever in the statute for appeal from the decision of the court martial. It seems to me cases of that hind should be tried before the magistrate under the proceedings 'by way of summary conviction, and if the young man were found guilty, and it was thought he was wrongly prosecuted, he would then have an opportunity of filing his bond and appealing to the judge of the county court, in the ordinary way in which appeals from summary convictions are taken. For that reason I would suggest to my hoh. friend whether the proceedings by court martial ought not to be limited to cases of desertion, after a man has actually become a part of the expeditionary force, and whether cases of mere neglect to report should not be tried under the Summary Convictions Act, in which case all the remedy ordinarily provided by law in case of summary conviction would be open to him.
Mr, MEIGHEN:	My hon. friend is not
quite correct when he says there is no appeal in the case of court martials.

There is none by this
measure. Where is that provision to be found?

Similarly, there is none in the ease of summary convictions. But the Code is still in effect and make3 adequate provision. There is also provision in the King's Regulations and the Army Act for a reconsideration of the sentence of a court martial. I am not very familiar with military procedure, but I understand-indeed, if I caught rightly the words of the leader of the Opposition, ihe stated the nature of the appeal in cases of court martial.

The sentence
is subject to revision by the military authorities.

There is a revision of
the judgment of a court martial. That judgment always comes before the competent military authorities including the Minister of Militia, so that it ie not correct to say there is no appeal in that case. On the main point raised by my hon. friend as to the wisdom of making a distinction in the tribunal in the case of a man who fails to report and in the ease of a man who having reported and having come under the jurisdiction of the military authorities, then deserts, I have made a note and will give an answer later on.

Will the section stand
in the meantime?
Yes.

The evidence takfcn before a court martial is all taken down in writing. This evidence, with the finding of the court martial, is sent, b.efore the finding is promulgated or goes into effect, to the officer who appointed the court martial, and the finding has to be reviewed and confirmed by him before it has any effect.
By him alone?

Yes. Afterwards it is
sent down to the Judge Advocate General at Ottawa, General Smith. That is a very long process, and unless the sentence is for a long period, any revision he made would not be effective. In the case of a long sentence, the Judge Advocate General is again charged with the duty of interfering if the sentence of the court martial does not appear to be in accord witlj the evidence presented. How far is it intended that this measure shall follow these soldiers? I presume it is not intended that there shall be one law for soldiers already enlisted or who enlist voluntarily, and another for soldiers coming in under this measure.

The point directly raised by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Taylor was in my mind when the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) was speaking and may be reserved for consideration with the matter already reserved at the suggestion of the hon. member for St. John.

In reference to clauses (a) and (b), is it intended that the penalty imposed in one part of the country for an offence shall differ from that imposed in another part of the country for the same offence? There seems to be some ambiguity in this respect. One court, for instance, might impose a sentence of twelve months, while another might impose a sentence of two years or three years. The sentence imposed in one province might differ from that imposed in another. The offence of desertion is desertion wherever it is committed. If a deserter is tried by court martial, the military authorities provide what penalty there shall be, but if say, in Ontario, a man fails to respond to the appeal of his country, he may have the maximum penalty of three years imposed. Some judge, however, in Manitoba or any other province might take a more lenient view of a similar case and might impose a smaller penalty. There should be no room for variation in the penalty imposed for that offence.

My hon. friend will see at a glance that it would not be possible to fix a hard and faet punishment for every case of desertion. A limit must be fixed and the decision left to the tribunal according to the circumstances. What may be a crime in one case may not be a crime of the same extent in another. There may be desertion and desertion, but very different degrees depending upon the circumstances of each case, just as in every case of the oommieeion of an offence.
I was not speaking so much with reference to the matter of desertion; I was speaking with reference to the man who does not respond to the call of duty.
That is desertion.

Then the men who will not respond to that call must, no matter where they may be, be treated in the same way. It might be possible for a magistrate, or

whoever tries the case, to impose a nominal penalty-
Three days instead of three years.

-of three days, or thirty day3 or sixty days instead of three years. The offence of not responding to the call should make a man liable to a fine consistent with the seriousness of the offence. I am not a lawyer, but there seems to be a wide margin for making a farce of the whole matter if a minimum penalty is not imposed for an offence of that kind.

The offence, like every other offence, may from an abnormity go down in degree of guilt and infamy until it is nearly nothing at all. For instance, if a man is a deserter, he may have such an excuse that the judge might feel is not a reasonable excuse within the meaning of the law, but is very close to a reasonable excuse. That man might come before the judge, and, while failing to convince him that his excuse is reasonable, might say: I am ready to submit myself right now; I would have done so before had I understood things. Would my hon. friend have the judge say to the man: Although you may be ready to become a soldier, I am bound to send you to jail for three years? I think what is in my hon. friend's mind is this, that a man having served his time would have expiated his offence and therefore not be liable again. He would be liable still. Were he sent to jail for three days, he would have' to report for duty immediately he was released. If he failed to do so, he would be again guilty of the offence.

Supposing you found in any particular district the officer trying the case not in sympathy with the principle of conscription or of military service, he might make a farce of the whole matter by giving offenders only a few days' imprisonment. There should be a minimum penalty.
The military authorities would soon get rid of such an officer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. member (Mr. Glass) does not recall the fact that the difficulty to which he alludes is experienced in the general administration of the criminal law. There are comparisons made -all the time in this country and in other countries between the sentence one judge may impose for a particular offence and the sentence another judge may impose for a like offence. You cannot regulate these matters in advance, if you are going 
to leave the degree of punishment to the judgment of the tribunal. Perhaps the hon. gentleman has not appreciated the observation made by the Solicitor General, that the imposition of punishment under this section does not relieve the man from his obligation to military service. He is still liable to it, although he may have received and undergone a sentence.
Is that made quite clear in the Act, and where is it to be found?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is to be found
in the fact that there is nothing in the Act against it. The man is made liable to military service. If he commits a certain offence he is to receive a certain punishment, within limits, but the imposition of that punishment does not relieve him from service to which he is liable under the provisions of the Act. It leaves his status in respect to the Act exactly as it was before.

I wish to support as
strongly as I can the suggestion of the hon. member for Middlesex. If the Act is to be really effective the clause should make an offender liable to a punishment of not less than three years and not more than ten or six years, as the case may be; that would be making it definite. The hon. member for Guysborough made a suggestion as to the expenses of incarceration of prisoners convicted under this Act. Personally, I do not see why a sentence of imprisonment with hard labour should not be imposed on any one found guilty under the Act. If the clause stands as it is, I think the salutary effects of this enactment will be frittered away. As the clause stands, a magistrate strongly opposed to imprisonment for this sort of offence-and they are to be found in all provinces-might let his personal feelings come into play and disregard the interests of the country. He might say with a smile to the man brought before him charged with an offence: " You are guilty. Three days in the common jail." Or he might sentence him to jail for only 2 hours. Surely, the Government cannot afford to allow an Act with such a clause to go on the statute-book. To my mind it would bring the Act into absolute contempt in many portions of the Dominion.
Would my hon. friend suggest that the Government be directly represented at the court?

My hon. friend is referring to the tribunal. My hon. friend

from North Perth had reference to the magistrate who tries the case.

I do not think he is paying much of a compliment to the judiciary of this country when he suggests that a judge would make light of this Bill, However, I should not object to seconding my hon. friend's amendment if he would also bring war grafters under this drastic law.

I am informed that a
session or so ago amendments were made to the Criminal Code dealing with th aft very class.

Have they been dealt
with?

I have not heard of
there being anything serious.

Some hon. members
have said the grafters should be shot.
Mr. BOYCE. I am in agreement with my hon. friend) from North Perth, especially, in view of the statement that an hon. member of this House makes in this morning's newspaper, that rather than obey the provisions of this Act, 20,000 or 25,000 people wpuld go to jail. That is certainly a serious statement to the public, coming from a member of this House. It makes one feel that we should be very certain with regard to the provisions in this Bill for punishment of any one disobeying the law in any part of Canada, irrespective of any province. Suppose that the threat of the hon. member-and his statement was made in public-were carried out and that 20,000 or 25,000 prosecutions had to take place, and that the magistrate who heard, the cases saw fit to impose a penalty of only 24 hours, those men would be getting off pretty lightly-
I am also inclined to support my hon. friend's general suggestion that the provisions of the Bill with regard to punishment do not go far enough. This is a very important measure, certainly the most vital measure that could be placed before this House and the country. It calls on every man, and the punishment for an offence should be so drastic that any one wilfully disobeying the law should practically be made an. outlaw. I would suggest-I will pffer no amendment now, as I understand the clause is to stand-'that any man who has been convicted should be deprived for a period of three years after his imprisonment of the rights of citizenship, of his right to v.ote, for instance, at either a provincial, municipal, or Dominion election because of his contumacious conduct in disobeying the law of his country which calls him out for active service.

As to the necessity for a minimum sentence I would ask hon. members very seriously to consider the purpose of the Bill. Its purpose is to make -soldiers, not jail-birds. If a minimum term is to be fixed and the contingency that -my hon. fiiend from Algoma suggests actually takes place, then the Bill will succeed in making jail-birds of these men, but it would be impossible under the Bill to make soldiers of them. We should bear in mind that immediately a man is apprehended for having deserted, by not reporting for duty, from that moment he is in the custody of the law, and whatever punishment he receives we have already made him an outlaw to the extent that he has disobeyed the law of the land. But as soon as he has served his term, be it only 24 hours-, he is under the Army Act in that he has deserted, and under the provisions of the Army Act he may be apprehended and brought before a tribunal and the law enforced; that is, he may be made a soldier; he becomes a soldier after becoming an outlaw. Keeping in mind what we have in view, and not the mere question of punishment, it seems to me that the Bill in that regard is as it ought to be. As to the necessity of a higher maximum of punishment that can be taken- into account with the other -suggestions made by the hon. member for Perth and the hon. member for New Westminster.

The answer of the Solicitor General has a bearing, of course, on the answer to the question I asked a short time ago as to how far this Bill follows the soldier. To my mind this Bill should not follow the soldier beyond his attestation. If we attempt to make it apply to him longer than that, I think we shall only be inviting trouble. We cannot have two classes of soldiers. We cannot have one law applying to men already in the army, and another law applying to those who are brought in under this Bill. If the Bill makes it quite clear that its purpose is to provide a force which is to be delivered over to the military authorities I think our trouble will be at an end. I would not for a moment group our citizen soldiers with the grafters to whom the hon. member for Rouville has referred.



I think it would be most unfortunate to stigmatize a man as a criminal because he 'has committed a purely military offence, such as failing to report,. When 1 had the honour of commanding a battalion in the Canadian *'Expeditionary Force, I had to do with a great many offences, against the military law. There was hardly a day a commanding officer's court was not held. In very few of those cases was there any vicious intent, and I found that the law of kindness was much more effective than [DOT]the law of repression, with respect to those soldiers; -and if you showed human sympathy with a soldier, and treated lightly an offence which was not repeated and recurring offence, explained to him his liability to punishment and the desirability that he -should maintain the dignity of his own institution, you got along indeed very well with him.
I should be sorry to, see any minimum punishment established under this Bill, as I think in a great many cases the purpose of the Bill would be served by apprehending the citizen and making him fully .conversant with the liability to which he was subjected under the law. [DOT]

I would suggest to my hon. Mend the Solicitor General that it might be well to have .some method by which a prisoner can be pardoned, provided that after sentence he should be willing to obey the law and become a .soldier. It strikes me that it would be well to have a provision of that kind, because no doubt there will be many cases of that nature, where men without very much intention of doing wrong fail to appear, and might be convicted and sentenced, and after spending a few days in jail might make up their minds that perhaps it would be better to join the boys in the fight, .and be willing to go. I would suggest that .some .person should have authority in oases of that kind to pardon a prisoner and admit .him into the forces.
In regard to the suggestion made by my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy) that a light sentence .might be imposed upon an offender by a friendly magistrate, which would, in .a way, make the Act a farce, I would ask would he not be liable for another .sentence? Suppose a call comes to John Smith to turn out on a certain day, and he declines to go. His .case is brought before a magistrate, and he is sentenced to, .say, a week's imprisonment. He serves his sentence, and is discharged. Is he liable to be called on again, or does that

settle the matter as far as he is concerned? Is he not liable for a second prosecution later on? I would .like to know from the Solicitor General what the .situation would be in a case of that kind.

He is liable in case of any future desertion. I would apprehend, however, that inasmuch as he is in the custody of the law he would he .physically under the military authorities, ,and it would be much more difficult for him to deseTt thereafter.
Would he not be liable to be tried by a court-martial, if the .magistrate was too lenient?
He could not 'be tried by court-martial for the same offence, no matter how leniently the magistrate may have dealt with him.
I mean, could he not be tried by court-martial the next time?

Yes. In case a man repents and changes his mind after he has been convicted before the magistrate and sentenced, the full power of pardon rests with His Excellency, and may be exercised. An Order in Council is now in effect covering convictions or desertions, which provides that the convicting magistrate or judge may, of his own motion, release a prisoner if the .prisoner is ready to take up again his military duties. That is to say, it has devolved upon the judge himself to provide more definitely for the pardon and release of men guilty of desertion, or guilty of absenting themselves without leave, which, of course, is another offence. In case of a conviction toy court-martial, there is full power to pardon, not in His Excellency the Governor General, but, I think, in the commanding officer. In any event, the members of the House who have more knowledge of military matters .may explain that it will toe quite within the power of superior .authority to release prisoners convicted by court-martial.

As the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) lias allowed members of the committee to ramble in the discussion of the Bill, I would suggest- we take up the question of tihe exemption of the clergy. I would not mention the point if my hon. friend the member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) toad not raised it in his speech this afternoon.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend had better let the matter stand. It will come up in its proper place. If we

begin jumping from one section of the Act to another, we will never get through.

Might I call the attention of my right hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden) to subsections 1 and 2 of this section. Does this wording mean that the appeal tribunals may also take evidence? I should imagine the intention is that only the local tribunal takes evidence. Or, is the court of appeal to take evidence also, upon the evidence already taken?
It was thought wise to give the appeal tribunal power to take evidence if it saw fit.
For what reason? It woul-d simply be a re-trial.

We want the very simplest procedure possible before the local tribunals; and we want as few lawyers as possible, the idea being that the great bulk of the eases will be disposed of by the local tribunals. It might be that under such conditions as that a man might not adduce before the local tribunals evidence that he later could adduce. We do not want to debar the court of appeal judge from taking that evidence if he sees fit.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER; The appeal will not be an appeal in the ordinary sense of the word, but the appeal court gives to the prisoner a re-trial before a judge.

Yes, much in the way
of an appeal from a magistrate under a summary conviction.
How many members of the appeal court will there be?
One.

Paragraph 2
says:
Any tribunal may hear evidence on oath or otherwise as it may deem expedient, and for the performance of its duties, shall have all the powers vested in a Commissioner under part one of the Inquiries Act.
You establish a court, but a, commissioner is not a court. Why this drafting? Why not say that the court shall have the power of a court of record?

A reference to the Inquiries Act will show that if the tribunal has the powers of that Act, it requires no more powers. I do not think it should be empowered further than a commissioner under the Inquiries Act. A general provision that it should have all the powers of a court of record would be more than would be necessary. It has hardly that status. It is more a board of inquiry than a court of record.
It is a board of inquiry, but it has power to give judgment. It is a board of iniquity .for the purpose of exempting a man,

Paragraph 2 of section
5 says:
Any tribunal may hear evidence on oath or otherwise as It may deem expedient.
Why "otherwise?"- It seems to me that this tends towards looseness of administration in the working of the tribunal. I think it should be confined to evidence upon oath or to a statutory declaration having penalties attached to the violation or breaking of the oath.
It might be evidence of affirmation.

My own idea was that it would be better that the tribunal should not be restrained in that regard. For instance, the cases might come very rapidly, there might be practically no question about a man's liability or about his right to exemption, and it seemed to me that it

would be better to leave it to the tribunal. If the tribunal thought the matter was sufficiently important, or the question sufficiently doubtful, to have an investigation, they could swear a man, but it might not be necessary to swear every man who wanted to make a statement before them.

What prompted me to make that remark was a story I heard about a certain regiment in a certain district where seven prospective recruits went before a medical board for examination. The officer who told me the story said that they were the finest looking body of men he had ever seen, apparently physically fit, all single, not one with a dependent, and every one was rejected.

A case like that would be taken care of by the presence of an official of the Department of Militia and Defence who could appeal immediately. I do not see that it will be taken care of any better by compelling swearing to the evidence.

My answer to that is that laxity in procedure would be bound to come from the lack of sanctity of the oath. If you establish the solemnity of the tribunal, you will get a better tribunal for investigating statements than by any other method or arrangement.
It will be left with the tribunal to make their own rules and regulations, and they can take evidence under oath if they want to. I agree with the Solicitor General.
Is it intended that parties appearing ljefore this tribunal shall be permitted to do so by counsel?

The question of practice and procedure is left entirely to the regulations and to that class of the regulations which are framed initially by the central appeal judge. He will deal with the matter of procedure entirely, and it will be left ultimately to his decision as to what provision, if any, shall be made for counsel.

I asked that question because subsection 2 says that:
Any tribunal may hear evidence on oath or otherwise as it may deem expedient, and for the performance of its duties shall have all the powers vested in a Commissioner under part one of the Inquiries Act.
I recall that a few years ago when a commissioner was appointed under the Inquiries Act to investigate partisanship, he held that he could not permit parties accused of partisanship to appear by counsel and in many instances they suffered to

a very considerable extent on that account. It should not'be left to the decision of a tribunal tout it .should be specifically stated in the Act or in the regulations.

That is the way it
will be.
Is it intended in the province of Quebec that a judge of 4he circuit court shall sit as a court of appeal over a judge of the Superior Court?

I do not see how that would be possible under the Act.
Mr.' DEVLIN: It is possible in this way. The local tribunal shall consist, in the province of Quebec, first, of a member appointed by the joint resolution of the two Houses, and .secondly of a judge of the Superior Court.
What tribunal?
The local tribunal.

Oh, no. We are at
section 5. We will discuss that when we come to section 6, but I do not think that is the case.

Referring now to paragraph 3 of section 5 I find the following provision:
The Governor in Council may, upon the recommendation of the Central Appeal Judge make regulations with respect to the establishment, constitution, functions and procedure of the said tribunals and such regulations may contain provisions for securing uniformity in the application of this Act.
That word " uniformity " is a very broad and elastic term. I do not understand how it can be defined. What is contemplated by that?

There is a similar provision in the British Military Service Act. The intention is this:	A very wide discretion is left to the tribunal under a succeeding section as .to exemptions. It is desired that the interpretation and application of those provisions shall be as nearly as possible uniform, and it was thought that the central appeal judge might draft such regulations as would look to the securing of the uniform application of these provisions throughout Canada. The very same provision exists in the English Act.

I asked that question because I thought that if there was a similar provision elsewhere we might know what it means and what regulations have been made. If there is a similar provision in the British Act, regula-

lations ought to have been made under it. What are they? I concede at once that it is desirable that there should he uniformity in the application of those clauses and that if possible the regulations should be made to secure that uniformity but unless there are precedents to which you can point, I am at a loss to imagine what regulations you could make which would be applicable to all cases beyond the com-monsense, prudence and fairness of the judges themselves. If you have any direction to give them, I should like to know if possible, what it is.

I think I should be
going beyond my rights here if I attempted to indicate what might be regulations; but I can easily imagine regulations that would look to uniformity. For instance it might be provided that the same rule in respect of the presence of counsel should prevail in Manitoba as in Nova Scotia, or that there should be uniformity in the application of the subsection relating to health and physical defects. It has been found necessary in other countries, and we have provided, that where a man is physically and manifestly unfit for military service he need not go through the nonsensical formality of going up for medical inspection. For instance, if a man had no legs the board could exempt him at once without his going before a medical officer.
Section agreed to on division.
On section 6, subsection 1:
The minister may from time to time by proclamation or otherwise establish local tribunals at such places as he deems necessary and give each an appropriate designation.

Will the regulations
referred to in subsection 3 be published in the official Gazette a sufficient time before the law becomes effective to permit the public to become familiar with the regulations?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It would be the duty of the Government to see that the people of the country had notice of those regulations.
Why is the word "otherwise" used, "proclamation or otherwise"? Is there any better way of making it known than by proclamation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know that there is, but we thought that we would leave it to the discretion of the minister.
I am afraid if he attempted to do it otherwise than by proclamation it would not be the best means of making it public.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That relates to the form of publication. There would probably be publication in the press and notices posted up.

Is this the subsection to which the ex-Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes) referred this afternoon when he said that military districts would be designated rather than geographical districts?
Some place in the Act I found it spoke of a provincial jurisdiction; I think section 7.

I can quite understand the point raised by the ex-Minister of Militia. Indeed, it was very frequently in our minds when these sections of the Bill were under review. The difficulty is that when it comes to the appointment of the Appeal Tribunal that is left to the Chief Justices of the provinces, and if it were done by military districts we should he under the necessity of having the 'Chief Justice of one province appoint the tribunal from another province.
Where will these tribunals be established? By counties? Where will they meet? It is important to know where the men will report themselves.	1

'The tribunals will not necessarily be established by counties. They will be appointed and the places Where they *are to meet will be set out.
5 p.m. There may be two or three tribunals in one county, one in another, and some counties may have none. The point at which the tribunal is first established will be selected so as to suit the convenience of the population. A tribunal may subsequently sit in another county, and its jurisdiction is .ample all over the province. Any person may appear before a tribunal wherever he is; but he must abide by whatever tribunal he selects.
Who determines the action of these movable tribunals?

The Minister of Justice. The intention is that if a tribunal finds it can do its work better in any other place it can wire for authority to move, and, having that authority, it may move to another place.
One tribunal might do the work for a whole province?
It might do the work for a very large area. Later on there is provision for the consolidation of tribunals, if lit is found that they are not all required.

What I had in mind was the convenience of those called. There may be in one township fifty young men, in another seventy-five, .and in another one hundred, and so on. The object of the Government will :be, no doubt, to cause the least inconvenience possible to young men and bring the tribunal as near to them as possible.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, that is the idea. That is why so much discretion was left to the minister, in order that he might study the requirements of population in the different parts of the country, and arrange the tribunals accordingly.

Subsection agreed to.
On subsection 3.-Local tribunals.

Judging from the remark just made by the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) I understand that a man may select his own tribunal. Suppose, for instance, a resident in Ottawa is conscripted, and wishes to appear before one of the tribunals, would he be allowed to present his case before the tribunal, say in the city of London, or the tribunals in Toronto?

Yes.
ii
Is that not an anomaly?

I think, as a matter of legal right, under this Bill, he would be enabled to go to London, and apply to the tribunal there, but the restraining circumstance is that he would have a lot more difficulty in presenting his evidence, and convincing the tribunal, than he would ii he applied to a tribunal close at hand. But what was sought to be avoided was the raising of questions of jurisdiction. If geographical limitations were placed on the jurisdiction of the tribunal, the question of the domicile of every applicant would come up, and interminable questions of jurisdiction would arise. Those are avoided by allowing the young man to choose any tribunal he desires within his own province.
There is no provision made .as to how many members will compose the Board of Selection?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, there is not, and I would be glad to have suggestions from hon. members. We had difficulty in
I Mr. Meighen.]
framing the section, and we desired to have it present not only the appearance, but the reality of perfect fairness to every one. Therefore, we arrived at the conclusion that a board of selection, established by joint resolution of the Senate and House of Commons, would be the best body. If any other course is considered preferable by the committee, I should be very glad indeed to consider it. We have the idea in our .minds that we might have a board consisting of two members from each province -18 in all.
Would that be two members from each province from the Commons, or from both Houses?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
They will not
necessarily be selected from the House of Commons. If they should be selected from the Parliament, of course it would be appropriate to nominate some members of the Upper House.

I have been thinking
a great deal about this clause-a little more than any other clause of the Bill-and my right hon.. friend must admit at once that a committee composed of, say, eighteen gentlemen from all over Canada would he a very unwieldy thing. There would be a very great deal of difficulty in getting them together, and I am afraid that many influences might be exerted upon them, and I would like to suggest, although I do not offer it as an amendment-that possibly there might b& a smaller board appointed for each" province in Canada, and see if that board, knowing the local conditions better than the larger board, could not work out a fairer method of choosing the members of these tribunals than could the general board that would be appointed under the suggestion of the hon. Premier. I simply throw out the suggestion. I think probably every member in the House has given this matter consideration. I know the people of the country have done so. I have received more letters along this line, and I have heard more criticism and discussion from people that I met and talked to on this phase of it, than on any other.
I think this suggestion might be worked out fairly well.

I have had
the same experience as the hon. gentleman from Carleton (Mr. Carvell). I expected that perhaps the Government had a plan of their own, but if the only plan they have at the present time is the one suggested, of having two members from each

province, I am afraid it would be am unwieldy body and the observations of my tan. friend from Carleton (Mr. Car-vell) appear to be unanswerable. Since the Government themselves are open to conviction upon this question, and ready to receive suggestions, perhaps the best thing to do is to reserve the subsection, and at the next sitting of the House tan. gentlemen can express their views on the question.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am not so
sure that it would not work out all right as it stands. As a matter of fact, it would probably work out in this- way: The members from each province would examine the situation in that province and arrive at a conclusion. Then the board would meet and make their appointments without a great deal of difficulty, because the gentlemen nominated by the members from each province would most probably be accepted by their colleagues from the other provinces. Therefore, the matter wmuld work out much in the way .my tan. friend from Carleton suggested, except that the appointment would be made by the whole board of eighteen, instead of by the local provincial board for each province. I shall be very glad to accept my tan. friend's suggestion and let the section stand.

One of the difficulties
would be that you could not find any two men in one province who are fairly familiar with every section of the province. My idea is that if you could have a hoard consisting of four or five members for each province, you would have a more representative board than one consisting of two members.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is well
worth considering. I had it in my mind that I w'ould ask my right tan. friend to name one man, and I would name another, and appoint the board in that way.
Section stands.
On subclause 1, of section 3:
1. In those provinces in which there are county courts or district courts, the county court judge or district court judge, or, if more than one, the senior judge for the county or district in which the local tribunal is established, or when the place at which a local tribunal is to be established is not within the territorial limits of any county court or district court, then by such judge as may be determined by the minister.
The judge making the appointment may appoint himself or any other judge having jurisdiction in the county or district.
For the purposes of this section, "county court judge" or "district court judge" includes
any deputy judge /authorised by law to act for the time being for any such judge, and also includes any acting judge so authorised.
In the province of Quebec:-
(a) In the judicial districts of Montreal and Quebec, any judge of the Superior Court of the province of Quebec who is authorized by the Chief Justice of the said court or authorized by the judge appointed to perform the duties of Chief Justice in the judicial district.
(h) In the other judicial districts the judge of the Superior Court of the province of Quebec assigned to the' judicial district within which the local tribunal is established.

According to part 2 of this section relating to the province of Quebec, a judge of the superior court shall appoint one pf the members of the local tribunal. Is that member of the local tribunal to be appointed by that judge to be a judge of the same court?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Not necessarily. It is
not contemplated that he would necessarily appoint a judge.
He may appoint any one?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: ' Yes.
So that the provision that applies to all the other provinces will not apply to Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is just the same as in the other provinces. There is no obligation in the other provinces for the judge to appoint a judge. There is a provision that he may appoint himself or any other judge, but as I understand the matter, he is not limited to appointing a judge. The matter is permissive as regards the other judges.

Is that limited only to
provinces other than Quebec? A judge in Quebec could not appoint himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is not provided that he might appoint himself, because I do not think it was contemplated that we would ask judges of the superior court to undertake the work pf sitting on the tribunals. In the other provinces the county court or district judges are to do the work, and it was thought it might be quite proper that a county court judge should be appointed to do that work, but it did not occur to myself, nor, I believe, to the gentlemen drafting the Bill, that there was any need of our setting.the judges of the superior court to do that work, because it is to be noticed that the appellate tribunal is to consist of a judge of the superior court, and it would be, from some points of view, undesirable that you should first have a judge of the superior court sitting on the local tribunal, and then an appeal from that judge of the superior court acting with

another member of the tribunal, to another judge of the superior court.

If I understand the
Minister of Justice aright, the Chief Justice of the Quebec district will make the appointments there and Assistant Chief Justice Archibald of Montreal, will make the appointments in the district of Montreal.
Mr." DOHERTY: Yes.
And in each of the districts of the superior court in Quebec, the judge ,of that district will make the appointments,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With this exception,
that in the districts of Montreal and Quebec, I do not think the intention is that necessarily the Chief Justice shall appoint, but he will designate one of his,judges to make the appointments.

The judge of the superior court may appoint himself or any other judge of the superior court or any body else.
Mr. DuHERTY: That is not expressly so provided, and the inference might, from the provision, being expressly made for the county court judges in the other provinces, be that the superior court judge would not be expected to appoint himself or another judge of the superior court. I pointed out a moment ago a reason why it should seem desirable that he should not do so. From that local tribunal composed of the nominee of the judge and the nominee of the board of selection, there is an appeal to a judge of the superior court. The reason why we have to make a difference with regard to Quebec is, as the hon. gentleman knows, that in that province we have no county court judges; we have only superior court judges.
We have judges of the circuit court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
