speechtext: Yes, but only in the city of Montreal.
It might be well to make a distinction there.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If the hon. member
thinks it desirable to make a distinct provision for Montreal, that question might be considered, but it seems to us that we should make a system of general application throughout the province. The judge of the superior court designated to make the appointments in the district of Montreal might, very properly, if he thought fit,

appoint one of the judges of the circuit court.	[DOT]
They are too. busy.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member suggests that our judges of the circuit court in Montreal have just about as much as they can do with their ordinary judicial work.

Does it not appear ridiculous to the minister that if a judge of the superior court is going to sit upon the local tribunal, yet afterwards under section 7, the Chief Justice may appoint, in the city of Montreal, a judge of the circuit court in appeal over the judge of the superior court?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did point out the fact that the appellate tribunal was to consist of a judge of the superior court as a reason why you should not put a judge of the superior court on the local tribunal. I think that the words " any court " probably ought to be altered. There may be something in the suggestion of the hon. member, and perhaps the matter ought to be made clear. I had not observed that; I had in mind, as working the thing out in Quebec, that we have, save in the exception mentioned, only the superior court, and there the judge would be a judge of the superior court. I think in that province the intention was that it would be a judge of the high court or the superior court that should sit on the tribunal. While I would not like to admit that the matter appears to be ridiculous as it stands at present, probably when we come to it, it might be well to amend the provision as regards that province.

In the subsection with regard to the provinces other than Quebec, the county court judge may appoint himself to be a judge. This is a very proper suggestion, because if there is in any place a man who would sit on these tribunals that man is the judge who administers justice generally. If we have not the same provision with regard to Quebec we shall be excluding the very men who are best fitted to sit on these tribunals. Subsection (b) of section II says:
In other judicial districts the judge of the Superior Court of the province of Queheo assigned to the judicial district within which the local tribunal is established.
If there is a man who ought to be a member of this court it is the judge in charge of the administration of justice

generally. If he is not allowed to appoint himself we shall be excluding the very best men we have.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As I pointed out, the judge of the judicial district will in all probability toe the appellate tribunal, and if he appoints himself to the local tribunal that will make it impossible for him to sit on the appellate tribunal. If he appoints himself to the local tribunal we should have a tribunal composed of one judge of the superior court and another gentleman named by the Board of Selection. They will sit and pronounce a decision, and that decision will be subject to an appeal to one judge of the superior court, and that one judge may reverse the decision of the district judge, assuming him to have a seat upon the local tribunal. What was in mind was that the judges of the superior -cuort were to constitute the appellate tribunal. That presents no obstacle in the way of a county court judge appointing himself to the" local tribunal, but it certainly is, 1 think, a serious obstacle to the judge of the superior court appointing himself to that tribunal, because in that case he would sit subject to an appeal such as I have indicated. There is no question that a judge of the superior court would be an excellent man to sit on a local tribunal, but on the other hand the general scheme does not contemplate the- local tribunal being composed exclusively of judges. It does seem to me that we can repose in the judge of the district court just the same confidence to make a good selection as we would repose in him himself if he were acting on the local tribunal, and that leaves his services available for the appellate tribunal.
Is it intended that one member of each local tribunal shall be a judge, or may the judge appoint whom he likes?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They can go outside the bench altogether.

When a judge has
selected the members of a tribunal, are they compelled to act?

Yes, subsection 5 of section 6 provides for that. In order that there may be no misapprehension, I may say that to my mind section 7 was intended to read exactly as it is. The provision enabling the Chief Justice to appoint appeal judges was made as wide as it is for the reason that in some provinces, particularly in the West and in outlying districts of
other provinces, the registrar might have very few appeals, and it would be very much more convenient to enable the county court judge residing in the district to hear the appeals than to send a King's Bench or supreme court or superior court judge from the capital of the province to hear those appeals. It was thought there would be no conflict of jurisdiction and no question of priority, at all events outside of the province of Quebec. A county court judge, even if he chooses to sit on one of the local tribunals, can only sit on one, and there would likely be several tribunals in his county. But, even if he sits on the local tribunal, we can trust the Chief Justice of the province not to appoint that particular judge to sit in appeal, and it is likely th^t no county court judge would sit in appeal over cases he had heard. I was not so familiar with the courts of the province of Quebec, and consequently no provision was made there enabling the superior court judges to appoint themselves. I remember that the point was raised, just as the Minister of Justice has raised it this afternoon, that the superior court judges would be those selected to sit in appeal, and the intention was that in each case they should make their own selection for the local tribunals and not appoint themselves.
Will tribunals be composed of laymen entirely, or of military men as well?
Civilian tribunals purely.
Is there anything in the Bill preventing the appointment of a military man?

It is not forbidden. The county court judge could select a military man as his representative, but it appears to me very unlikely that he would do so or that the board of selection would choose a military man.
I was under the impression that one member of the local tribunal was to be a judge, and the other member appointed by the board of selection.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: One member is appointed by a judge.
But apparently that is not the intention. I suppose that no judge would be appointed on the local tribunal?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
He might or
might not be. The local tribunals will have to be numerous, for the convenience of the population, and for that reason it would

be impracticable to have them composed of judges or even to have one member of each tribunal a judge.

There may be good
reasons for not having judges on the local tribunals but I was under the impression, and I think the public was too, that one member of each tribunal would be a judge. With regard to Quebec, a judge may appoint himself or another judge, but in all probability he would not appoint himself or another judge when he could appoint a layman. So I look forward to having these local tribunals composed of people other than judges. There is nothing whatever in the Bill, so far as I can see, preventing a military man from being a member of a local tribunal, and I do not see what warrant the Solicitor General has for saying that a county court judge would not appoint a military man. The Bill does not prohibit it.
I do not see why military men should be debarred. It - does not matter whether they are military men or not so long as they are not partisans; that is the main thing.

Has the minister considered the advisability of providing that there shall be a judge on each tribunal? It occurred to me, when I first read this section, that the county court judge would appoint either himself or another judge. That is perhaps a strained construction, and the Solicitor General says that that is not the intention. Have the Government considered the advisability of providing that one member of these tribunals shall be a judge?
That could not be done if there was only'one judge in the county.

I realize that difficulty, but I should like to see the tribunals composed of men in whom the public have absolute confidence, and against whom there would be no suspicion whatever. In th'e great majority of cases, I am sure, the men appointed by the county court judge would be the very best selection he could make, but sometimes the county court judge might have great difficulty in finding men of the proper standing in the community who were willing to act.
I have looked over my own constituency, and I have wondered where in the world I could find a man who would be willing to accept that responsibility. I am afraid we will have some difficulty. Of course, I realize it would be imposing a very great burden upon county court judges, because

in our province one judge has charge of three or four counties, and he would have some difficulty in moving around all over the country. In any event, I wish the Government would consider that phase of it.
Does that refer to the local tribunals?
Yes.

It seems to me there would be difficulty in working it out in the West. In all southern Manitoba from Saskatchewan to Winnipeg there is one county judge only. In the constituency of Souris there is no judge.
In all probability the territory would be too large to have it work satisfactorily.

Is it the intention that there should be one local tribunal for each county? Clause 1 of section 6 says the minister may, from time to time, (by proclamation or otherwise, establish local tribunals at such places as he deems necessary. I would like to know if it is the policy of the Government to appoint one local tribunal for each county, or if it is proposed to establish more than one, where the county is large? If more than one were appointed it would avoid inconvenience.

It would be impossible to define exactly how many would be appointed to so many miles, but I have not in mind at the present moment any county where one tribunal would be sufficient. The county most familiar to me, of course, is Portage la Prairie, and I know it would be utterly impossible for one tribunal to take care of that county. Men would have to travel seventy miles to reach the tribunal. Such a thing would be absurd in a well-populated county. Consequently, it might be fair to state that there will likely be a local tribunal appointed in every substantial village, unless it happens to be very near some larger place. The aim is to meet the convenience, of the people, and to avoid, as much as possible, imposing expense and loss of time upon them.

Might I suggest to my
bon. friend that, as it will be rather difficult to find the proper man to act on those tribunals-and I do not suppose there will be any great enthusiasm to go on the boards-that- the selection of the judges be made from the justices of the peace of the county. These gentlemen have a fair knowledge of the law, and enjoy the confidence of the community. They are per-

feetly acquainted with the districts in which they live, and it seems to me they are the men 'best fitted to come in contact with the (public and to give the Act a fair trial.

I have no doubt at all
the justices of the peace will be called upon. They have a great deal of experience in the matter of hearing evidence. At the same time, I think it would be very unwise to confine- the selection to them.
I might take this opportunity of saying that since the outbreak of the war members of the Government, and members of Parliament as well, I have no doubt, have been in receipt of very -many communications from prominent citizens all over Canada offering their services free. Those gentlemen are actuated by patriotic motives, and nothing else. They are anxious to do something in the war. I am in hopes that from the best of that class of people we will be able to get the men who will carry out the work of those loeaT tribunals, and carry it out well. To all those who have made such offers, and their number is thousands, I extend an invitation now to make it known that, if chosen by the authorities, their services will be available for this work. If they do, we will obtain very excellent results indeed, and I hope there will be no shirkers from the- duty of performing the work of the local tribunals any more than there will, be shirkers from those who should enlist for the war itself.

I would not make the
fact that a man was a magistrate a disqualification, but I would not like to make it a supreme qualification either.

Well, I should think
not.

These men must have
, other things to recommend them besides being accustomed to taking evidence. They would have to be fairly good students of human nature, men with very level heads, men who are unswerving in their views and who are absolutely fair.
I would like to ask the Solicitor General if he has had any- communication from the Motherland as to the success of their tribunals, or the satisfaction they are giving in their methods of operation. The reason I ask this: two gentlemen who have been in England told me within the last ten days that the work there in this respect was very unsatisfactory. I would not state the particulars, but they assured
me that if the same method was followed here, and the same lack of wisdom, I would say, in the performance of those duties, the whole thing would be quite unsatisfactory.

We have various reports as to the working of the tribunals in England. What my hon. friend says is something similar to the reports we have received; subject to this modifying fact, while at first their local tribunals were unsatisfactory mainly because they seemed to think that in certain districts it was their duty to accept everybody, or to reject everybody, still they profited by their experience. They have had no less than five Service Acts introduced in the British House, three of which are now law. Each of these Acts took advantage of the experience they had gained under the preceding one. Now, we think we have taken advantage of all their Acts and all the experience they have had under them. One of the difficulties they had was that their tribunals were too large. We have profited by their experience in this connectioin. They also realized that the fullest opportunity for appeal had to be given to the military authorities. We think we have covered that also. Then, again, they have not a full control of their procedure as they moved along. We are in a position to enable the tribunal to have full control of their procedure, and there is a provision in our very first Act for uniform procedure. Consequently, if they have met with very many difficulties, we have no reason to believe we will meet with the same.

How many exemptions

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend must be guilty of not having read the Militia Act very carefully. The power conferred upon the Governor in Council by the Militia Act is infinitely greater than that proposed to be conferred by this Bill. The idea of naming a judge was to remove the exercise of power from the Government and thus to avoid any suspicion of partisanship and to restrict the Government to such regulations in the respect mentioned as would be recommended by the central appeal judge. It could not be said that the Government were enacting regulations on their own initiative, but solely on the recommendation of an absolutely independent and impartial authority. Look at section 144 of the Militia Act and see the power that is conferred by that section:
The Governor In Council may make regulations tor carrying this Act into effect, for the organization, discipline, efficiency and good government generally of the militia, and for anything requiring to be done in connection with the military defence of Canada.
You cannot imagine anything wider than the powers that .are vested in the Governor in Council under this section. Anything that is proposed in this Bill is infinitely short of that and moreover we have restricted the power of the Government in so far as this particular matter is concerned by requiring that the Governor in Council shall act only upon the recommendation of an independent judge, a man of whose impartiality and good faith there could not be the slightest possible suspicion.
Do I understand that the recommendation of the central appeal judge will be accepted by the Government as recommended? Do they reserve to themselves the power of supervision?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We do reserve the power of supervision but it comes to us as a recommendation from the judge and we cannot pass it unless he has recommended it.

The judge makes the recommendation and that recommendation may be accepted or not accepted by the Government. The regulations may be amended. I do not know how it is in the other provinces but in Quebec the rules of practice made by the judges are not subject to revision; they are a law unto themselves. If the central appeal judge were empowered to make rules that were binding, that could not be revised, then, I could understand the argument of my right hon. friend; but that is not the Bill. The Bill says that the judge can make recommenda-

The Chief Justice of the court of last resort in each province, or in case of his absence, or failure to act, then, a judge of that court designated by tire minister, shall establish for such province a sufficient number of Appeal Tribunals, and shall assign to each such tribunal one judge of any court of such province, and shall distribute among such tribunals all appeals from, and cases stated under subsection two of section ten, by local tribunals of which the. registrar has notice and such appeal tribunals shall severally hear and decide the same.

I am in favour of the coordination of all the strength of the nation, to win this war, and I would not have any clause in this, Bill saying that even a Chief justice eould fail to act, even if he did not want to. If he was in good health I would see that he was not absent, and if he was present I would see that he acted- We are passing' a compulsory measure, compulsory for the men who have to risk their lives, and I would, not leave it optional to any man, even as high as a Chief Justice, to say whether he would act or not. I would make it part of his duty and make it compulsory for him to act.

Section 7 is a very vague statement. Are these appeals to be established by the Chief Justices and not by this Parliament? Are the tribunals to he composed of one, two, or three men? The Solicitor General this afternoon intimated that he supposed these appeal tribunals could really hold new trials, that they were not simply courts of appeal. From reading the Bill, I understand that the court of appeal was to revise the decision of the local tribunal. I do not object to the view of the Solicitor General that new witnesses could be heard. But it seems to me that this section should define clearly the character, composition, and jurisdiction of the court.

It defines its jurisdiction and its composition. It does not say how many tribunals shall be established in any province. It says that the Chief Justice shall assign to each tribunal one judge of any court, and shall distribute among such tribunals all appeals, etc. That establishes the jurisdiction and the power. The only thing that is not definitely fixed is the number of tribunals, and that could not be fixed until we knew the nuimber of appeals. We assign to each tribunal one judge of any

court; the number of members of the tribunal is fixed, .and the jurisdiction and powers are fixed. As soon as the registrar gets all of the appeals collected and the data for the appeals, he allocates those appeals geographically for the province, 9 p.m. and then the Chief Justice of the province, who will have all of that information, will assign a judge of any court to try these appeals. The judge so appointed can not onljr try appeals in the strict sense of the word, 'but can also hear new evidence. It would be unwise to prevent him from hearing new evidence for the reason, among others, that it may not be found necessary to take down all of the evidence verbatim at summary trials.
As to the point raised by the hon. gentleman from Renfrew, I have absolute confidence that there is no possibility of any chief justice in Canada failing to perform his duty, unless some disability prevents his acting. It is impossible to conceive of the chief justice of a province of Canada failing to perform his duty, and it is a duty of the same character as those he is performing weekly in the discharge of the duties of his office. In the province of Manitoba, the number of sittings of assize is fixed by the judges themselves, according to public necessity. The same character of duty is assigned to the chief justice here. I cannot conceive that any one would fail to discharge his duty. If I thought that were possible I see no reason why provision should not be made for it.

I do not want to say anything about the members of the Bench, because I have the greatest respect for them, but there are times when they consider their convenience is almost superior to the convenience of the public. I have seen this feature in cases in which I have been interested. The fishing might be particularly good at a certain time of the year when this Act ought to be put into operation, and they might delegate this work to some person else as an ordinary duty, so as not to interfere with other arrangements. I am not saying it disparagingly, but if there is a loophole left for that, we might have the chief justice doing the work of some other judge, who might do this work just as well. My viewpoint is that this, being a compulsory measure, should not be left to the option of any judge, whether he is chief justice or not. The law should say that he should act, and that it was part of his duty to act. It is a time for sacrifice for all of us, and, as the Solicitor General says, the chief
[Hr. Meighen.]
justice would not shrink from the duty, except under some circumstances, where he might think the duties to be performed would be performed just as well if relegated to some other member of the bench. I should say that the chief justice ought to act. Some of our chief justices have been very pronounced in saying that a conscription measure ought to be passed, to make men go to the front. I would make it apply to all these men in favour of conscription.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is imperative.
Except in .eases of " failure to act."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is all that can be said of any of the judges or chief justices. Of course, in case of failure of a judge to perform his duty he may be impeached. In addition to that, there is a provision in the Criminal Code under which a man who refuses to perform an obligation imposed upon him by statute is liable to be prosecuted before the courts, if necessary.
But he will not be.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If we inserted such a provision here, would it be more likely that he would be?

In regard to the other tribunals, if a man fails to act, unless for some good reason, he can be fined a sum not exceeding $500, and the Solicitor General is considering the advisability of making the penalty more severe. But with respect to the chief justice we hesitate to say anything, except that we provide a remedy if he does not act. He is relieved, and the minister appoints another judge to take his place. I cannot get away from the fact-and I think none of us can-that this is not the ordinary Criminal Code or Judicature Act, or whatever you wish to call it; it is a compulsory measure.
Conscription of men.

Every man who is asked to perform any duty under this Act ought to be compelled to perform that duty. I would make no distinction between the case of the chief justice and men assigned to any other tribunal. I would make it read "in case of failure to act from illness," or something of that kind, but not broader than that. The ordinary person reading the Act will say, "Well, when it came to the chief justice, they did not apply the rule to him that they have to all other men supposed to be engaged in this great struggle." Nobody ought to be excused, according to my judgment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is a difference
between the members of the ordinary tribunals under this Act and the chief justice. The obligation on the others would only be created by this statute. That office is created and the obligation is created to accept it, and then you make a penalty for this new state of affairs that never existed before, but youT chief justice is an officer bound to perform all the duties imposed upon him in his
quality of chief justice, and liable to certain consequences for failure. You are imposing an additional duty on him, and all the consequences of failure to perform any duty attaches to him.

You would
impeach him?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would not say what we wpuld do.
With reference to the provision about the court of appeal. I understand the court of appeal is to be composed of only one judge, to be appointed by the chief justice.
Yes.
And he is to have jurisdiction to try the case?
Yes.

One feature which might defeat the object of the Bill is the multiplicity of appeals. We have first, if I understand well, the Ipeal tribunal, then the appeal tribunal, then the central judge. I stated the other day, repeating what my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) said in his address to the House, that there was, in that multiplicity of appeals, a chance for a rich man who wished to escape as much as possible the obligation, which the poor man had not. I do not raise the issue for-the pleasure of raising it, or to create a prejudice in the minds of the public.
But I say that unless it is made very clear that the deposit which is ordinarily required for the lodging of an appeal will not be exacted in either case and that the- cost of those proceedings will be reduced to a minimum, there will exist that prejudice in the minds of the people. If the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General would make those two points very clear the people would be impressed with the idea that rich and poor alike can, if they have a just case, not only appear before the local tribunal, but go to the appeal court and the Central Appeal Judge. There is a subsection in the Bill which enacts that the regulation for the setting in motion of those appeals will be prepared by the Governor in Council.
Will toe approved toy the Governor in Council.

Clause (b) of subsection 3 of section 10 says:
The Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Central Appeal Judge, may-make regulations governing the right to and fixing the conditions of appeal from an appeal tribunal to the Central Appeal Judge, provided

any person authorized by the Minister of Militia and Defence may as of right enter and prosecute such appeal.
Before this Bill is passed, the Governor in Council, that is to say, the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General, ought to provide the tribunals referred to in that clause, so that the public may know that there will be no undue favouritism on behalf of a certain class ..of the community as against another, so that the people of this country, rich and poor alike, will be on a footing of equality. The Minister of Justice, who has had long experience as a judge, knows that it is very easy to create an injustice by exacting from a poor litigant a large deposit to bring his case to appeal. In Montreal, where my hon. friend has practised law, and where he has administered law for so many years, there are classical cases of rank injustice where the litigants had not the means to go to the appeal court. I do not suppose the cost will foe high, but we live in a time when the cost of living is high, and when the people have not too much ready money. This, is not an ordinary piece of legislation.
The usual administration of justice has to look after only a few litigants, but here you have the whole nation which is liable to be called out, brought, so to speak, automatically before those courts. In the name of common sense and justice, I appeal to the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General to frame, before this Bill is passed, regulations which will show clearly to the people that there will he no high cost for the setting of the machinery in motion, and that the deposit to lodge the appeal will be practically nil.

I can set my hon. friend's mind at rest on both points immediately before any regulations are made. There will be no deposit at all required for appeals, and such regulations as provide days, times, procedure, etc., will be such as to reduce to the very minimum, if not entirely to eliminate, the necessity of costs. The object of the regulations will be to make the appeal just as acceptable and just as applicable to the poor as to the rich.
Will the appellant have to forward his case and the evidence to Ottawa, or will he have to go there himself?

The first appeal is to the appeal judge, and the appellant can take new evidence to that judge or he can give his evidence over again. There are 
no strict rules as to that, and that judge will be almost as convenient to him as the local tribunal. It is hoped, at least, that there will be no necessity of a man going very far to an appeal judge. No fewer appeal tribunals could possibly be established than three. He who objects to three tribunals has not thought the matter out or does not weigh his words at all. It is hoped that the first court of appeal will weed out the number of appeals to a relatively small number. It is inconceivable that any one central tribunal at one time could hear all the appeals that will be made inasmuch as there is the utmost freedom of appeals. One court would never get through all the work. Consequently, there has to be an intermediary court, and no one could suggest anything else that would properly handle the appeals and at the same time that would be practicable in its working. There are two appeals in England and two in New Zealand.
How many are there in the United States?

I do not know. The regulations on this point have not yet been received. The appeals could not be simpler than they are here, and all that is left to the regulations is as to the right to appeal and the conditions of appeal. We had not in mind financial conditions, but simply the rules to be followed which will be of a very general and simple character to enable each appeal to be prosecuted with the least possible expense and to be disposed of as expeditiously as possible.

Does not section 7 lay itself open to this criticism? It says:
The Chief Justice of the court of la*t resort in each province .	.	. shall assign to each,
such tribunal one judge of any court of such province.
That might be a county court judge. Might not this situation arise? The local tribunal might consist of a county court judge and a layman, who would give their decision in regard to a man's exemption. There would be an appeal from their decision. Under section 7, might not the Chief Justice appoint a county court judge of another county to hear an appeal from a judge of the court of the same jurisdiction and a layman? That would be a rather ridiculous situation. Should not there be in the section something to state that in case of an appeal from a local tribunal consisting of a county court judge and a layman, the appeal should be

to a judge of 'a higher court? There is no provision except that the Chief Justice shall distribute the appeals. A county court judge of Oxford county might set aside the decision made by a county court judge of Middlesex and a layman. We do not think the Oxford county court judges are more capable than those of Middlesex.
Why not say in the Act that he shall do that?

If we had provided in
*the Bill that wherever a county court judge -site, even if on only one case, a judge of the King's Bench must be sent to review it, we should be imposing very great inconvenience for very small cause. It seems to jne that the way in which the Chief Justice will naturally get over the difficulty will be by assigning these cases to be tried [DOT]by a judge in a near-by place. He knows the amenities of the Bench; he understands the feelings of judges as to being tried by their equals, and he, of all men, can be trusted to have regard to those considerations in the disposition of judges in courts of appeal. I do not think such cases are likely to arise at all, although they are possible under a strict reading of the Bill, I do not think in the first place that the Act need be worked to avoid that condition, because I think the judge will avoid it, and in the second place, I do not see how we could very well word the Bill so as to avoid it.

Did I understand the
Solicitor General to say that the appeal court will consist of only one judge?
Yes.
That would be an argument against appointing judges on the local tribunal. It would be much cheaper to appoint a county court judge to hear the appeals.

lit is an argument, I
think, against compelling judges to- -act on the local tribunal.

I cannot understand why the Solicitor General does not even want to inconvenience a judge of the King a Bench, This Act is to compel men to risk their lives, but the Solicitor General wall not use compulsion on a chief justice. He hesitates -even to compel a county court judge, and he does not want to inconvenience-that is the wordheused-ia member of the King's Bench. I-jvould not look at it in that light. I would make this a compulsory measure, and if it was necessary I would send a member of the higher courts anywhere, however much it inconvenienced him. I would make this measure compulsory on every person it affects.

It is not regard for -the judges so much as regard for th-e public that governs. Judges are fairly busy, or are supposed to be. In the province of Saskatchewan, for instance, they are not merely busy but -actually congested -for reasons that I need not expatiate upon here. Litigation is very much in -arrears; there has been a congestion there for two years. It is not in the public interest that for an insufficient cause one of these judges should be compelled to lose days -and -perhaps weeks doing something that could very eon-vi-ently be done by a -county -court judge on the spo-t. The judges are, of course, compelled to -act when they are needed, but we are -not coimpelling the -chief justice of -a province to appoint one judge instead of another, when the other might be m-u-ch more convenient to the locality; that is tall. The compulsion is on the chief justice just as it is on every one else, and the compulsion- is on the appeal judge when

he As appointed by the chief justice. The penalty lies in the law as it stands to-day, and a judge who refuses to act as liable to a much more severe penalty than -any one As liable to who is nominated and fails to -act on a local tribunal. The penalty of $500 is very small compared with what a judge of the court is liable to if he fails to do his duty according to the statute.
You would force the appeal judge to go to the district to hear these cases, and not make the applicants go to him?
He would go wherever he was sent. The appointment will be fixed conveniently to the residence of the appellants.
You will see that that is carried out?
Oh, yes.

I cannot follow the argument of the Solicitor General. He is considering the convenience of the public entirely, he says, but his whole argument tends to convince me that he is serving the convenience of the judges. The judges in this country are paid well in proportion to the amount of work they have to do, and I do not think they are overworked. They may do their duties well; I am not saying anything about that, but here we are dealing with the liberty of the subject, the thing most dear to all men. The Solicitor General should provide in the Bill that in case a county court judge is a member of a local tribunal, appeals from that tribunal shall he heard either by two county court judges or by a Superior Court judge, no matter how much it inconveniences them. This is a very important measure; we are at war; we are calling out men and sending them to fight and die in foreign lands, and at a time like this the convenience of a chief justice or two county court judges should not be considered. The Solicitor General must admit that we have a great many more county court judges in the province of Ontario than are necessary to do the work.
I think other provinces are in the same position. I repeat that if the Solicitor General is unwilling to inconvenience a Superior Court judge, the appeals should be heard by two county court judges.

The suggestion of having two judges looks to me as possibly being practical. I will see if it can be arranged for.

Mr. J. A. DESCARRIE-S (Jacques-Cartier) (translation): Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a point clearer which, in my opinion, is of the greatest importance: I refer to the appeal taken to the appeal tribunal and then to the central appeal judge from the judgment which will be given by the first tribunal. Should this not he put in the Act? When the law is sanctioned and enforced and (difficulties arise, it will be too late to provide a remedy, whereas such difficulties could easily be obviated now. Why do you not say in this legislation that, in those appeals to the first appeal judge or to the central appeal judge, the appellant will have the right of producing new evidence?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not see any objection to that, but neither do I see the necessity for it, as that point is governed by the regulations which are to be made by the Governor in -Council on the recommendation of the central appeal judge, and it seems to me that the hon. gentleman could accept our -assurance that those regulations will provide for such cases as he refers to; the more so as it would not be practicable to apply to such appeals, under that Act, rules of procedure applying to civil cases, in which a record is made and prepared before the judge of the lower court.	The
fact must not be lost sight of that proceedings before tribunals of first resort are summary proceedings, and I have but little doubt that were it left to the

decision of the appeal judge, seeing the great similarity of the proceedings "with the proceedings in appeals in criminal matters -the judge would decide that it is absolutely necessary for him to hear new evidence, as no docket is prepared in writing which could be handed over to him. It seems to me that the hon. gentleman could accept the assurance that this will be made absolutely clear by the regulations and that he will have in those regulations which most control the procedure, exactly what he desires.

My hon. friend was not here this afternoon, when this matter came under review, and if he looks at section 5, he will find that not only the appeal tribunal has the right to hear the evidence, but the three tribunals.
Here is the English version:
5. (1) There shall he established in the manner hereinafter set out the following tribunals:-
(a)	Local Tribunals;
(b)	Appeal Tribunals;
(c)	A Central Appeal Judge.
(2) Any tribunal may hear evidence on oath or otherwise as it may deem expedient, and for the performance of its duties shall have all the powers vested in a Commissioner under Part I of the Inquiries Act.

I would like to leave with the Solicitor General for later consideration the suggestion of empowering appeal tribunals to appoint counsel to represent appellants, these counsels to be paid, of course, by the Government. I make this suggestion largely for the purpose of eliminating any excessive costs, or any costs at all, on the part of appellants.

Why would my hon. friend limit it to appellants? After a case had been decided by a local tribunal, or by the appeal tribunal, the Minister of Militia might carry it to the central court of appeal at Ottawa, and put the subject to any amount of expense in defending the judgment he has obtained. I think there is a great deal to be said in favour of the suggestion of my hon. friend, but I would not limit to appellants. In every case I would give the subject the right to counsel. Of course, this comes up a little more prominently in section 10, which contains a most extraordinary provision, giving to the Minister of Militia the right to appeal. He may carry a case from the local tribunal up to the central appeal judge. He has the right to appeal, as a matter of course, and he need not give any bond or furnish any security for costs. If the subject has obtained a judgment in the lower court, the
minister may practically ruin a poor man, carrying him from court to court without any possible redress.
I think the suggestion of my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) is a very excellent one. If there is a provision for the benefit of the sulbject, whether he is an appellant ox a respondent-
Of course, I mean that.

I would like to get some information from the Solicitor General as to when this right of appeal begins, and what t'he appeal is from. It is not very clear from what the first appeal is taken. As I understand subsection 2 of section 4, after a certain proclamation is promulgated everybody in a certain class becomes subject to military law. There is no selection in the body of men called out by that proclamation. There may be hundreds among them who will not pass the medical examination, but they are subject to military law the moment they are called out. Of necessity, there must be some of them who will not find it necessary to appeal, because the medical examiner will turn them down. Are they supposed to appeal then to this central tribunal, before the doctor passes judgment upon them, or are they to wait until they are declared medically unfit? I have not been able to understand that very clearly. Perhaps the Solicitor General will make it definite as to when the right to appeal begins in the case of a man who is called out under the proclamation
The right to appeal begins immediately the decision of the local tribunal is obtained.

Whether exemption has been granted, or refused?

tary discipline. Immediately on reporting he goes before the medical examiner, in the usual way, and if he is found unfit for service that ends it. His duties, under that call, have (been answered. Clause 7 stands. We
do not ask that the clause shall be passed.

I do not think there
is need for more than one registrar in a province, and I do not think it is advisable, having regard to uniformity. Have you provided for

Regarding the appointment of a registrar in the province of Quebec, there are two important and well defined [DOT] judicial districts in that province, those of Montreal and Quebec. The chief justice of the Montreal district visits the Quebec district and the chief justice of the Quebec district visits the (Montreal district.
