speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I suppose it
would be possible to apppint a deputy to the registrar for one of these districts if it should be found necessary.
Mr. McKENZIE .[DOT] What are the duties of these registrars?

Mr. MEIG-HEN: The principal duties of these registrars are to receive and to allocate appeals geographically throughout the province in order that the chief justice may appoint judges to try those appeals with convenience. .
On section 10-Appeals:
10. (1) Any person aggrieved by the decision of a local tribunal, and any person authorized by the Minister of Militia and Defence, may appeal against any such decision.
(2) If the two members of a local tribunal cannot agree as to any decision to be made by them, they shall forthwith state in writing the case to be decided and cause the statement to be sent to the Registrar for the province in which the tribunal is established.
(3.) (a) Subject to the provisions of paragraph (b) of this subsection there shall be an appeal from any appeal tribunal to the Central Appeal Judge.
(b) The Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Central Appeal Judge may make regulations governing the right to and fixing the conditions of appeal from an appeal tribunal to the Central Appeal Judge, provided any person authorized by the Minister of Militia and Defence may as of right enter and prosecute such appeal.
(4) The Central Appeal Judge shall be the tribunal of last- resort, and the Governor in Council may, on his recommendation, appoint one or more other judges of any superior court to assist the said Central Appeal Judge in the discharge of his duties, and define their powers.

The first subsection gives to the Minister of Militia the right of appeal. It does seem to me that when a man has applied for exemption on the ground of sickness, infirmity or any of the other grounds which are set forth in the statute, if the Minister of Militia desires to appeal from the decision in the case, it should only be upon terms prescribed by the appeal tribunal. It is hardly right that the Minister of Militia, having authority to employ counsel and having the money of the country behind him, should put the subject, who might be very poor-perhaps utterly unable to employ counsel, and who might be affected very grievously by the cost of the proceedings that he would have to take to defend the judgment which he has obtained from the local tribunal-to the trouble and expense of defending a proceeding of this kind. It would be unfair that as a matter of right the Minister of Militia, without any conditions, any obligation as to cost if he fails, should have the right to enter an appeal. This right is still more objectionable when we come to paragraph (b) because (b) provides that the central appeal judge may make regulations governing the right of the subject to appeal. The Solicitor General stated that it was only
intended to fix the conditions of appeal, but it is his duty to make regulations limiting the right of appeal as well as fixing the conditions. It is his duty to
-make regulations governing the right to and fixing the conditions of appeal from an appeal tribunal to the central appeal judge, provided any person authorized by the Minister of Mi-lita and Defence may as of right enter and prosecute such appeal.
Why should there be a greater privilege extended to the Minister of Militia to carry the appeals from one court to another than is extended to the subjects who have obtained judgments in the first instance from the local tribunal? It does seem to me that it ought to be entirely the other way. The subject ought to have the right of appeal but if the Minister of Militia is not satisfied with the judgment of the local tribunal he ought to be compelled to enter into a certain obligation; at all events, to save the subject harmless of the costs incurred by reason of his being compelled to go from court to court until finally the Minister of Militia might carry him before a judge of the Supreme Court in Ottawa and might involve a young man in expense and hardship that would be almost ruinous to him.

On this subclause 1 which we are at present discussing, the right of appeal is a free right of appeal on the part of both from the local tribunal. There is no restraint. But, under subclause (c) of section 12 it is provided that:
The Governor in Council may make regula-. tion	under which application for certificates may be made, deferred applications received, appeals entered and heard and rehearings had.
That is to say, conditions might be fixed, not conditions that would become a restraint, not conditions that could not be filled by either ithe individual applicant or the Militia Department. There might be conditions that could be easily complied with. It was felt that the central appeal judge might well make -such regulations as would, in isome way, limit appeals from that appeal tribunal to the central appeal jndge. But it would be impossible to limit the appeals from the Militia Department, because in no other way could we secure that uniformity of application throughout the Dominion that is so desirable. My hon. friend isays there should be even a freer right of appeal from that tribunal to the central appeal judge on -the part of the individual than on the part of the department. At the opening of tlhe discussion this afternoon, my bon. friend from

Renfrew (Mr. Graham) made some reference to oiur taking (advantage of the experience of (Great Britain in this regard. It is the experience in Great Britain that we have Ihad regard to* here. The experience there of the permission to appeal equally on the part of both to the central tribunal in London proved very disadvantageous in the obtaining of the necessary men under the Act. It caused great delay in many oases. So we have deemed it wise to enable the (central appeal judge to make such regulations 'as, while they are quite fair and -will cover all necessary and proper oases, will not allow an unrestricted right of .appeal to every one, which would practically suggest and would perhaps break the whole machinery. There is no hardship involved. Every man has the right to appeal to the judge of a court of ihis own province, and he must be aggrieved by a judge of that court before he can complain.

The Solicitor General
states that the regulations governing appeals are to be made by the .central appeal judge.
Governing the right to appeal from the (appeal tribunal.
That would be so if it depended entirely upon section 10. But by subsection (c) of section 12, the Governor in Council is allowed to make regulations. The two provisions seem to be inconsistent.

What is contemplated in section 12 is the entering of appeals, meaning the initiation of the appeal in the first place. It may be well to consider, when we are dealing with section 12, whether that should not also be among the regulations to be first initiated and recommended by the central appeal judge.
The Solicitor General says that it is desirable to discourage appeals.
Not quite.
Well the experience in England has been that appeals have caused delay.
That is from the appeal judges.

It seems to me that unless we know the nature of the conditions of appeal that would be fixed by the Governor in Council, we can hardly tell whether it is going to remedy the evil or

not. It may be that the condition of giving a bond as security for costs would operate very advantageously to the wealthy man, who could easily furnish 10 p.m. his bond or security for costs, and very disadvantageous^ to the poor boy who wished to carry his case to appeal. We have no intimation what those conditions are to be. The Solicitor General has not answered the argument that the Minister of Militia should have no more right to carry the subject from court to court without any obligation to give security for costs, or making any provision for giving the subject the advantage of counsel, than the subject would have to carry his appeal from court to court. Take the case of a young man who has made application for exemption. He gets a judgment from the local tribunal in his favour. The Minister of Militia, without giving any security, without any condition whatever being fixed, may appeal from that judgment to the appeal tribunal. If he gets a judgment from the appeal tribunal overturning the judgment of the local tribunal, then you are making provision under which the Governor in Council, upon the recommendation of the central appeal judge, can prevent that young man from appealing to have the judgment of the local tribunal restored. You are going to take away from him that right, while on the other hand, after the subject has got judgment of two courts in his favour, you allow the Minister of Militia to carry him off to the central appeal court without providing any security for costs, and without any conditions in respect to the appeal. It seems to me that is imposing an unreasonable hardship upon the subject. If there are to be any conditions attached to the appeal, those conditions ought to apply equally to the Minister of Militia and to the subject; indeed, I think they ought to apply much more strictly to the minister than to the subject.
There would be no object in having security for costs put up by the Minister of Militia.
Make him liable for costs.

It is quite within the power of the central appeal judge to provide by regulation that in appropriate cases, looking to the means of the applicant, compensation can he granted to any one who, in his judgment, is unnecessarily brought before the central appeal judge.

It is quite within his power, under clause (b), subsection 3; section 10. I think that is quite adequate. At all events, the experience of Great Britain shows that unless the right of appeal is given the Militia Department to the central appeal judge, this measure will be in great danger of failing of its primary object.	_

I submit there is no fairness at all in that clause. There are two paddies to the suit, the conscript and the Minister of Militia. Each has the right of appeal. If the minister is given the right of appeal he should be on a parity with the conscript, and should be subject to all the rules. If the minister is exempt from furnishing bonds, or giving security of any kind, the conscript should not be placed in a worse position. The rule should apply to both; there should be no exception. An appeal is given from the local tribunal to the appeal tribunal and the party has simply to say: "I appeal." When you come to an appeal from the appeal tribunal to the central judge, conditions are imposed upon the conscript, but not upon the Militia Department. I do not know what the conditions will be. It is provided in subsection 3 of section 10 that regulations can be made limiting the right to appeal. One condition may be the furnishing of a bond or making a deposit, or there may be a limit of time. But the conditions, whatever they are, will have to be performed by the conscript, whereas the Minister of Militia will be free from all those formalities, and can simply walk into court and say: " I appeal." That is not fair at all. They should be on an absolute parity in both cases, and I do not see how my hon. friend can justify the greater restriction upon one than upon the other.
The hon. gentleman is not quite correct in saving that there can be no conditions places upon the Minister of Militia in reference to an appeal.
The section says so.
No. *
How do you construe the regulations?
The regulations may provide conditions, but they must not be such as to prevent the absolute right of appeal.

Paragraph
(b) of subsection 3 of section 10 reads:
The Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Central Appeal Judge may make regulations governing the right to and fixing the conditions of appeal from an appeal tribunal to the Central Appeal Judge, provided any person authorized by the Minister of Militia and Defence njay as of right enter and prosecute such appeal.
That gives the Minister of Militia the right to enter and prosecute an appeal, without conditions.

I can only give my interpretation. I cannot say it is worth any more than the interpretation of any one else. My interpretation is that conditions may be imposed in reference to carrying on an appeal. Those conditions may even be applicable to the Militia Department, but there must not be such conditions that will put it in the power of any one to prevent the Militia Department prosecuting the appeal. They may compel the Militia Department to fulfil certain conditions, or they may compel them to provide for the witness fees of the other side, but they cannot prevent them from prosecuting the appeal, whereas these regulations may provide a condition, applicable to the individual, that he shall be prevented from prosecuting an appeal, except with the consent of the appeal judge. Such a condition, under this clause, could not be applicable to the Militia Department. Condition might be made -which should be performed by the Department of Militia, but not a condition which would prevent the Minister of Militia, in any case, going to the Central Appeal Judge. They cannot do anything that puts it in the power of any one to prevent him appealing, but any other condition would be quite a fitting obligation.
Mr. PUGS.LEY: They can take away the right of the public to appeal?
They can.
That is putting him in a difficult position.

I do not contend they are in the same position, and I only say, in defence cf that, that if we are to have regard to the working out of the British Act at all, and if we are sincere in our desire to get these men, the working out of the British Act has shown that it will not do to have the parties on a parity with regard to appeals to (the final court-that there must be as much freedom of appeal on the part of the Militia Department as there was in Great Britain, which will enable them to go to the final court, thus

assuring the uniformity of application everywhere, and securing the men. I do not contend that they are on a parity, but I say it is necessary that the free right of appeal should exist on the one hand, and I do not think it is necessary on the other.

That is where we disagree. I do not know what the regulations may he, but I imagine that perhaps it might not be contemplated that the right of appeal from the appeal judge should exist as a matter of right. That is the party may be compelled to present a petition to a judge, making a prima facie case, giving some reasons why the appeal should be allowed. I can conceive of such regulations being made, but no further than that. In the case of the conscript, when he comes into court, they say to him, "You want to appeal? On what ground?" He may say, "I want to have a new witness," and he may be allowed to appeal upon certain conditions. But, on the other hand, the Minister of Justice walks in, without giving any reason at all, and says to the court, "I appeal this case, I have no reason, to give;" -simply "I appeal." Notwithstanding what my hon. friend may say as to the necessity and advisability of administering this Act so as to get recruits, it is repulsive to one's sense of justice that one side should have more privileges than the other. All classes should be on a parity, and if one side hag to fulfil conditions in order that he may be allowed to appeal, the other side should be placed in the same position. It seems to me, as the provision stands, it is against the rules of fairness, equity and justice.

The two are not on a parity, in the first place. The country is acting for everybody. The individual is acting for himself; and, in the next place, conditions might be imposed which would compensate the individual for the harassment of an unnecessary appeal, such as the provision that the conscript's expenses should be paid by the Crown. You could not, on the other hand, impose similar conditions on the public, because it would be immediately said, "You are making it possible for the rich man to appeal to the central judge, but you are making it impossible for the poor man." In a word, it is impossible to impose the same conditions on the individual as you may impose on the Militia Department. Consequently, as the conditions cannot be the same, the rights cannot be the same, because the individual is acting purely for himself. On the other hand, the Militia Department is

acting for the whole countrj, and they do not start out on a parity.

I have no objection to that. On the contrary, I am quite disposed to agree with my right hon. friend that these appeals should be as simple as possible, devoid of formality, going direct to the question to be decided and dispensing with law if possible. But in the Bill as it stands, the firet appeal is without any formality at all; it is. of the character represented by my right hon. friend. The conscript walks in before the judge and says:

"I appeal." He may say to the judge: "I have a witness whom I had not at a former trial, and I want to have him heard." But when you come to the second appeal, here is the condition which I read in the Bill:
The Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Central Appeal Judge, may make regulations governing the right to and fixing the conditions of appeal.
The very fact that the judge may make regulations governing the right of appeal nullifies the object my right hon. friend has just stated. At once there must be formalities. The judge makes regulations to limit the conscript's right to have his appeal. What are those regulations? I wish we knew them, but they are left to the judge. They may be of one character or of another character, but whatever they may be, I sulbmit as a matter of equity, justice and fairness, that the rules which are imposed upon the conscript for the exercise of his right shpuld also be imposed upon the Minister of Militia, and vice versa; otherwise, there is no equity in the matter at all.

Subsection 2 of
section 10 provides for a stated case in the event of a disagrement between the two members of the local tribunal. Is that subsection complete in drafting, .or is there some other section in the Bill, which I do not know of at the moment, which deals further frith this matter?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, section 7
says that the cases so stated shall be heard.
That is complete, yes.

Subsection 2 of section 10 provides that if there is a disagreement between the twomembersof the local tribunal, they shall state a case which they shall transmit to the registrar of the province in which the case arises. It is the duty of the registrar to turn that over to the appeal court, but there is no provision made for transmitting the evidence taken by the local tribunal along with the stated case. The evidence should go forward with the stated case, so that the court of appeal would have an opportunity of seeing what evidence was taken before the local tribunal in order to arrive at a decision.
_ Sir ROBERT BORDEN: In stated cases, you do not require evidence.

A stated case would
embrace such a summary, of the evidence as would make the appeal intelligible to [DOT]the appeal tribunal. We could not impose
upon the local tribunal the necessity of including all the evidence in a stated case, because that would .involve the necessity of all the evidence in every case being taken down in writing.	.

But nothing is said
about the evidence going forward?

A stated case cannot
be anything other than, a 'Statement of the evidence in the case, a short statement, signed by the two members of the tribunal of the facts as brought out in the evidence.

I am not objecting to the central appeal judge having the right to make the regulations governing the right of appeal, because that is where your frivolous objection comes in. But assuming that the Crown exercises the right of appeal, and the man has received a decision in his favour before the first tribunal, unless some means is provided he will be unable to follow up that appeal. He might have a perfectly just case, but, having no means to defend himself, the case would go against him.

I had that very case in contemplation, namely, an appeal by the Militia Department from the decision of the appeal tribunal. I can conceive that there would be cases where the central appeal judge would decide that equity demanded compensation to the individual who was brought before the central appeal judge or some other judge named by him.
Are you referring to the taxation of costs to the conscript after the appeal is heard?
That is what I referred to.
I was referring to what might happen before the appeal was heard. If a conscript has no means he would never be able to get before the central appeal judge.

I was just proceeding to that. There might be a case where, owing to the capricious action of the official of the department, a man who was appealing a case might be put to an expense that he should not have been put to. That might very well be covered by regulation. I do not see how it could be covered by the Bill, because a great deal would have to be left to the central appeal judge himself. There might be cases where the individual might not be able to get to the central appeal judge or some other judge named by him, but those cases would likely be very few, because the central appeal judge has power to name some judge in British Columbia, Nova Scotia, and so on, to do the work for him, and consequently the expense could not be so great. It would appear to me best to leave to the central appeal judge the framing of the regulations under which indigent cases, so to call them, might be provided for. If we inserted in the Act a provision that a certain sum shall be lodged in the event of an appeal by the Militia Department we should

be putting a very high premium on appeals beyond the tribunals. We want to discourage such appeals as much as possible. I do not see why the central appeal judge could not Ibe trusted to work out some regulations for payment for the service of subpoenas and such other necessary costs as he might feel ought to be provided for, on the production of evidence of inability to pay on the part of the applicant.

I do not think my hon. friend is following me. I am not pleading for the applicant, but for the man who has received a decision in his favour from the tribunal, and against which decision the Crown has appealed. If this man has no means he is unable to carry on the case. My hon. friend does not live in a part of the country where they have a divorce court, and so he does not know what real justice is, but down in the Maritime Provinces we have a divorce court and the wife has a right to demand that the husband who is suing for divorce shall pay her costs day by day, or the case cannot go on. I think that might be done in this case where the Crown is appealing against the decision from a court below.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is not done in divorce cases alone. Sometimes an appeal is granted, by special leave, to the Privy Council upon condition that the appellant in any case shall pay the costs of the respondent. There might be regulations which would restrict the Minister of Militia in that way, and it may be very desirable that there should be such regulations to cover some cases; that is to say, if a case is decided against the Department of Militia by the tribunal, and it is desirable for the purpose of securing uniformity of decision in all the provinces that there shall be an appeal against that decision, it might be possible to provide that in any event the Minister of Militia shall pay the costs of that appeal.
That is what I am contending for.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It does not seem possible to provide for that in this Bill. It had better be left to regulation.

I do not care whether it is done by Bill or regulation, so long as I am assured that it will be done. But if it is not in the Bill it is possible that the central appeal judge might not consider it necessary to put it in the regulations, and in that case, although we all have the best

intentions, the poor man would be without redress.
That clearly should be done by regulation. The appeal judge would consider the wisdom of such a course and what the costs should be.

Do I understand that a man will be allowed to appeal from the decision of any army doctor? A doctor might pronounce him physically fit, but the man himself, guided by his own feelings or the advice of some other doctor, might declare that he was physically unfit. Could he appeal?

There is no appeal
from the opinion of the army doctor as to physical fitness. The man would be in just the same position after the decision of the army doctor as he would be in to-day.

I have listened to the discussion and am unable to come to any conclusion whether or not the Government intends to give to the conscript the right of appeal to the Central Appeal Judge. I should have thought that the real object of having this appeal judge was to enable the Minister of Militia to get uniformity of decision throughout Canada. The Solicitor General has rather admitted that the regulations may take away the right of appeal altogether from the subject.

Except in certain
cases.

Would those cases be appeals on question of fact or on questions of law? Reading the whole section one must be struck by the anomaly of it. Section 3 (a) says:
Subject to the provisions of paragraph (b) of this subsection there shall be an appeal from any appeal tribunal to the Central Appeal Judge.
That clearly limits the right of appeal. It does not give what one would think was being given to the subject, namely, the right of appeal. Section 3 (b) says:
The Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Central Appeal Judge, may make regulations governing the right .... of appeal.
Under that, it seems to me that the judge can make such regulations as will actually deprive the subject of the right of appeal, either on a question of fact or on a question of law. It goeS on:
-provided any person authorized by the Minister of Militia and Defence may as of right enter and prosecute such appeal.
The effect of that is the regulations may absolutely deprive the subject of the right of appeal to the central judge. The Minister of Militia has an absolute right pf appeal, which cannot be taken away from him under those regulations. I only wish to Tepeat what I said before, in the hope that some weight may be given to the suggestion. It is only adding to what has [DOT]been said by my right hen. friend who sits on my left (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that if a conscript has had a judgment of the local appeal tribunal in his favour, he ought not to be carried to the central appeal judge by the Minister of Militia, without some provision being made to reimburse him for his costs, in case the judgment appealed from should be sustained. My hon. friend says the desire is to discourage appeals, but, as has already been pointed out, it is not the case of the conscript appealing, but of the Minister ,of Militia not being satisfied with what might have 'been the judgment of two tribunals in favour of the ^subject and he still wants to carry the case to a higher court where the conscript may be absolutely unable to meet him by reason of his poverty-and where on account of the case being undefended, the Minister of Militia may get a judgment reversing the judgments of the inferior courts. This is contrary to the principles of natural justice, and should not be permitted. If the subject has a judgment of either one or two of these courts-appointed in the very careful way in which the Prime Minister says the tribunal is to be appointed-I say it is grossly unfair that the Minister of Militia should be permitted, as of right, to carry the case to a higher court without making any provision which would enable the poor boy-who possibly, is absolutely without means-to meet him in this higher court. There should be either an equal condition of affairs as between the subject and the Minister of Militia, or there should be, in the case of the minister appealing from the ' judgment of one or two of the inferior courts, some provision which would do justice to the c.onscript in the way of guarding him against the loss which he must necessarily sustain.

I do not disagree altogether with the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) that there will be cases of unfairness if entirely unrestrained by any condition the Minister of Militia were to have the free right of appeal against the judgment of the two courts below, but there is nothing in the Bill which says that he must have such right of appeal unre-

strained. All I argue is that the central appeal judge can better frame the provisions which seem fair in his judgment- the conditions that must toe lived up to by the Minister of Militia-before he allows an appeal of the Minister of Militia from the judgment of the lower courts.
According to subsection (to) the right of the minister to appeal is without condition.

The central appeal
judge may make regulations governing the conditions upon which that right may be exercised. He cannot prevent the Minister of Militia from exercising it, but he can hedge it around with conditions which the minister must fulfil, such as, for instance, a provision for witness fees.
Or, depositing a sum of money for the costs?
Exactly. So that he is quite at liberty to protect the subject against embarrassment, so far as money can protect him.
Then, why not say so?
If my hon. friend can frame a clause which will take care of cases of that kind, I will be quite open to receive it.
I have it framed already.

I never claimed that
exactly the same right of. appeal rests on the one side as on the other. The Militia Department represents the whole people of Canada, and the individual represents himself. It is not a principle of law that the same right of appeal rests on both sides. Rights are presumed, and rights are granted under the common law of the land, in favour of the Crown, which the" individual does not enjoy.
' Mr. PUGSLEY: In what case? Will the minister give an instance?

In the collection of
debts claimed by the Grown, the Crown has a right which the individual does not enjoy.
That is very different.

The Crown has the
rights in this country and in Great Britain which the individual does not enjoy at all; and why? Because it is in. the public interest. The Crown represents the people, whereas the individual represents himself.

In a trial between two individuals there must be an absolute parity, but it cannot be in the interests of the State that in a contest between the State and the individual there should be a parity in .all things. I contend those very principles .should be embodied here.

There was a
time when the Crown had more rights than it has to-day.

Very true. It might be that, under this, regulations may be adopted whereby the consent of the appeal judge must be secured before an individual can take a case to the court of appeal. It might be, that consent would be called for where it was .a question of law, bult not of necessity, where it was a question of fact. Such, restraints would be fair, reasonable and right, but you could not geit uniformity if the same restraint were applied to the Militia Department.

The reason
given by my hon. friend is 'that it is essential to have uniformity. That is not the reason at all.
It is not the only one.
It is the principal reason, as I have understood.

My hon, friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) wished to know how we could provide for what we are seeking. It seems to. me that I would like to make this proposal.
Paragraph 3 (a) says:
Subject to the provisions of paragraph (b) of this subjection there shall be an appeal from any appeal tribunal to the Central Appeal Judge.
I would suggest that at the end of that clause you put these words:
Provided that if such appeal is prosecuted by the Minister of Militia the latter shall be required to deposit with the court such sum as the judge may direct to pay the costs of the respondent to such appeal.
That would not meet the very case that the hon. member has in mind. Where would the respondent get his money in the meantime to carry on his fight?
He knows that the Government is putting up the money and he will probably find some enterprising ba"-rister who will help him.

Will he not be just as well off if the regulations provide that if

the cost of the appeal is harassing he will be recompensed?
If the minister will say that the regulations will contain that provision I am satisfied.
If his right depends on his being successful, I do not know that there will be very much protection for him.

If he wins there is no provision by which he will get his costs. He may win in every court but the statute gives him no costs. I cannot see where, under the statute, the central appeal judge can make regulations which will give him his costs.
That is the intention.

Then there should be an express provision to that effect. It does seem that the minister is carrying it too far when he says that the spirit of the statute is in the interest of the public and against the subject. Every statute passed for the protection of the subject is said to be in the interest of the public. Every criminal law is, and we know that the criminal law is always administered with the most tender regard for the subject. The subject is at an enormous disadvantage as against the Crown.
Why then is the subject not given the same rights to challenge before the jury as the Crown is giving to stand aside jurors?

Because under the law of Canada there must be a unanimous verdict of the jury of twelve before a prisoner can be found guilty. That is an enormous advantage. That advantage has been taken away from the prisoner in many countries, amongst others in the United States, because in some of the states nine jurors can find a prisoner guilty. In this country there must be a unanimous verdict.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The verdict has to be unanimous here either for conviction or acquittal.
That is absurd; if the jury do not find a unanimous verdict against the prisoner they are discharged after a reasonable time and the man goes free.
What about a disagreement? They might bring in a disagreement. It is just as fair for one as the other. But as to the right of challenge, the advantage is given to the Crown in every trial.
No.
It has the right to stand aside jurors.
In a capital case, a case of murder, . the prisoner can challenge twelve jurymen and the Crown can only challenge three. Is that not so, Mr. Minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think those figures are correct.

The Crown can stand
aside a hundred if it likes.

The Crown simply
stands aside so many until the panel has been gone over, but when the clerk begins again tp call the panel the Crown has a limited right of challenge. I think it has only one-third or onie-fourth the right of the prisoner.

The right of the Crown to stand aside jurors is practically an unlimited right in Manitoba and other prp-vices and it gives an enormous advantage to the Crown. That principle pervades our civil as well as our criminal law. How could it be contended that the two stand on a parity before the cpurf?

Any man who has had
anything to do with the administration of the criminal law will recognize that the law is always tender and merciful to the accused. He is deemed to be innocent until proved guilty. He is given the right to challenge twenty jurors While the Crpwn has only the right to challenge three. There must be a unanimous verdict of guilty before the prisoner can be found guilty and condemned to punishment. The Crown has a most tender regard for the rights of the subject and the reaspn is that the subject is at an enormous disadvantage. In this case, here is the Minister of Militia with all the poweT and authority of the Crown, and with all the money of the treasury at his back, with power to employ counsel and to call witnesses frpm all over the country, while the subject, the conscript, who may be without money, notwithstanding that he may have got judgment in two courts, may be dragged to Ottawa, before the central appeal judge without any provision for the payment of his witness or counsel, or even his travelling expenses. That is placing the subject at an enormous disadvantage and it is contrary to the spirit which hitheTto has animated Parliament in connection with any Bill that I have ever known to be passed.

I did not intend, as was suggested by my hpn. friend from Cape

Breton (Mr. McKenzie), that this sum of money would only go to the respondent in case he won. The amendment was drafted very hurriedly but my intention was to so draft the clause that this would he a sum of m.oney set aside to pay his costs, win or lose. If he loses the Crown gets his body. It is only to put an indigent person in a position to defend himself.
It applies to every case whether he is rich or poor.

Certainly. I take the
ground that if the Crown appeals a second time and the respondent has the decision below, the Crown should pay the costs of the appeal.

Mr. Chairman, I approve the suggestion made by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). Since the Minister of Militia who, in the main, is the Government, is not obliged to make a deposit in order to proceed with his appeal, it seems to me there is no reason to compel the appellant, who believes himself wronged by conscription, to make a deposit as a security for his appeal costs. Otherwise, it would be debarring from their right to appeal a large number of people who might think they had been wronged by the local tribunal's decision. There will certainly be appellants among those who will be in the first class and there will also be in that class young men twenty years old. Now, I wish to point out that, in the province of Quebec, a youth of twenty is a minor, that consequently, he has no rights, or responsibilities, in order to obtain money. He cannot legally contract a bond or a security in order to make a cash deposit to allow him to appeal. I will go further and say that the greater part of these young men are absolutely resourceless. Then, do I ask, how could these young men appeal when they feel they are wronged, if they are deprived of all means to do so?
Would there not be some way of protecting these young people, who are at the start of life, who have no earthly possessions and not even the legal capacity to contract, would there not be some means of giving them at least the right of appeal of course without any expensive procedure, of paying only their witness costs, in fine, that they be only liable for those things which they would absolutely be obliged to do for themselves? I make this suggestion in order to protect this most interesting class of young men, the first youth of the country who are to be called upon to fight

for the protection of our rights. Therefore, at least, let those who would believe they are injured by conscription have a chance to appeal to the highest tribunal and to do so in a practical manner, that is to say, let us afford them the means of doing it without compelling them to fill certain conditions which they are unable to fulfil.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I may say, in
reply to the hon. gentleman that it has already been stated that there is no intention whatever to exact deposits as conditions for appealing. In the next place, the terms to be laid down must be couched in the form of regulations which will be prepared by or at the suggestion of the court itself (Central Appeal judge). I believe we may depend upon the court and that they will not attempt to lay down conditions which the appellants would be unable to comply with. If we can trust the court as regards the settlement of the main issue, it seems to me we should be thoroughly satisfied that they would not impose conditions which the appellants could not possibly meet.
At all events, hon. members have suggested the imposing of conditions upon the Minister of Militia, as to the costs and expense, but there is in the Act nothing to suggest that pecuniary conditions would be imposed upon the appellants.

I have perfect confidence in the decision to be- rendered by the tribunals as to the merits of the appeal, but as to the conditions we do not know what they may be. It is perfectly possible that the appeal judges impose as a preliminary condition of such an appeal, a deposit, a security of some sort, or such other conditions which would be so burdensome that those parties of whom I was just speaking, those twenty year old minors, would not be able to meet them, it would be. like shutting the door upon them. It seems to me that Parliament, that the members have the right to know whether the conditions to be imposed by the judges and ratified by the Governor General in Council, shall be burdensome to such parties or shall give them the opportunity to appeal.

This Parliament and all parliaments have been in the habit of [DOT] enacting substantive law by the Act itself and not leaving it to regulations to be dealt with in regulations. In subsection (b) of section 3 the Solicitor General is departing from the ordinary rule and leaving the enacting of substantive law to regulation.

The right of appeal is substantive law. How we shall get to the court of appeal, etc., is a matter of regulation, but the right of appeal is substantive and should be enacted by this Parliament. While I am very anxious that everyone should have all proper rights of appeal, my criticism of this Act is that it provides for too many courts, and none of them strong. It would be better to have a court of first resort stronger than any courts I have heard mentioned yet, and let that be the end of it. The matters that go to that court are covered by subsections (a) (b) and (c) of section 11. The county court judge and another man sitting with him will not be a strong court to deal with the subjects that must necessarily come under 'those sub-sections, and it would be better to have a strong court of first instance composed of men capable of dealing with this broad subject. I would say, let that strong court deal with it once for all, and do not let us have this irritating condition of going from one weak court to another. I am not reflecting in any way upon the capacity of judges; but these are not matters of law; they are matters of the common utilities of the country, and a judge is no better able to deal with them than anybody else. If the plan I have suggested were adopted, there would be less irritation, less trouble and a better administration of-justice.

Reverting to the question of challenge, I find that a person
charged with an offence punishable with death is entitled to challenge peremptorily twenty jurors and the Crown only four, not three as I said.

I quite agree that in regard to challenge more liberty is given to the accused, because the right of telling jurors to stand aside is practically unlimited on the part of the Crown, and is a very powerful weapon. It must be remembered that those provisions are modified by provincial legislation, at least on the point of standing aside.

The right to stand aside continues only until the panel is exhausted. The provincial legislature in the constitution of the court may increase the number of jurors; perhaps that is what my hon. friend refers to, as that increases the number who may be stood aside. But that is only until the panel is exhausted, whereas the prisoner's right is to challenge peremptorily, and, in addition, he can challenge for cause.
I understood from the Minister of Justice that the appellant would not be obliged to make a deposit in order to make his appeal good. Am I right?

Not the individual.
Progress reported.
